4153d31aa986cd67: MUNICH: Bayern Munich's star striker Harry Kane pledged to return for the "business end of the season" after undergoing surgery on his left ankle on Saturday.
Kane limped off after 20 minutes of Bayern's 1-1 home draw with Cologne in their Bundesliga match on Friday, with the club confirming the England captain had torn a ligament in his ankle.
Bayern issued a statement on Saturday saying the Ballon d'Or winner had "successfully undergone surgery" on his left ankle.
"The 33-year-old will now begin his rehabilitation programme," Bayern said, with the injury expected to keep Kane out for three to four months.
Kane posted a picture on social media from his hospital bed on Saturday, vowing to work his way back to fitness this season.
"The highs and lows of life! Obviously very disappointed to get this injury, but as always it's an opportunity to show resilience and improvement going into 2027.
"I'll be back fresh and ready to go for the business end of the season."
Kane shared a quote from three-time Super Bowl-winning wide receiver Julian Edelman: "Tough times don't last, tough people do," while thanking fans for their messages of support.
Kane has a history of ankle issues, although he has only missed a handful of games since moving to Bayern in 2023.
England coach Thomas Tuchel will be keeping a keen eye on the rehabilitation progress of England's most capped player.
England play Norway in the Nations League quarter-finals in late March.
The injury comes at a difficult time for Bayern, who are currently missing several players, particularly up front.

Bayern are without Luis Diaz, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, Ismael Saibari and captain Manuel Neuer, while midfielder Jamal Musiala and coach Vincent Kompany both returned after long lay-offs on Friday. — AFP
857ca6fed7d22775: LANGKAWI: Wearing khaki trousers, a sleeveless shirt and riding a 13-year-old bicycle, 60-year-old Ariffin Abdul Manan defied convention to complete the IRONMAN 70.3 Langkawi today.

Despite limited training and modest swimming skills, the former tour guide from Jerantut, Pahang, clocked seven hours, 19 minutes and 57 seconds to finish ninth among 14 competitors in the men's 60-64 age category.
The race comprised a 1.9km swim, a 90km bike ride and a 21.1km run.
For Ariffin, crossing the finish line meant delivering on a challenge set by his son, who registered him for the race.
"I am happy I did not disappoint my son, who registered me for the event. It is not easy to finish this event as it is my first 70.3 race.
"I knew my training was not enough. I am thankful for reaching the finish line safely.
"That alone is enough to make me happy. I managed to complete all three disciplines before the cut-off time," he said.
Ariffin said swimming was the toughest leg as he is not a strong swimmer, alternating between breaststroke and freestyle to cover the distance.
"I really do not know how to swim well. When you move slowly, your body feels heavier, and it took me quite a long time to finish the swim," he said.
He also had to run in thin shoes he was unaccustomed to, though he finished without developing blisters.
"Something new for me today was running in these shoes. They are quite thin, too, but thankfully everything went well.
"If I had developed blisters, I would have taken them off. Even if the organisers disqualified me, I would not have minded because blisters are really painful," he said.
Ariffin, who took up running about 20 years ago to quit smoking, rode an old bicycle he bought from an Australian friend for RM3,500 in 2013.

8f3767ab4d594407: SEREMBAN: Negri Sembilan police have yet to receive a report from Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim over an alleged resignation letter submitted to the palace without his knowledge or consent.

c2dbd0063ccaa486: KUALA LUMPUR: The wife of a senior fire officer reported missing in Nepal has spoken of the distress caused by repeated calls and threats from parties seeking to recover her husband's debts.
Hani Othman, 40, said she first received calls from an e-commerce platform company in October informing her that her husband, Mohd Fakhrul Munir Mohd Isa, had outstanding payments.
"At the time, I explained the situation, including my husband's disappearance, and they asked me to submit the relevant documents via email.
"Although I had submitted the documents, I continued receiving calls threatening me with payment demands, even though I had already explained the circumstances," she said when contacted recently.
She said the calls had become increasingly frequent, with more than 10 calls a day from the parties involved.
"It's not that I don't want to settle the debt, but I am facing difficulties because I cannot access my husband's bank account to make the payments.
"They call me more than 10 times a day. I feel distressed when I am contacted and threatened over the debt every day," she said.
Hani said her husband did not have many outstanding debts, while his bank loan repayments had been granted a moratorium until February 2027.
"To be honest, I have come to terms with my husband's disappearance. However, I hope the families of others involved in the incident will have their affairs eased, including their financial matters.
"I believe many other families affected by the incident are facing similar problems, adding to the difficulties of managing their daily lives," she said.
She said the family was still waiting for official confirmation from the Nepalese authorities on her husband's status.
"Although DNA samples were submitted early in the incident, we have yet to receive an official announcement or written confirmation from the Nepalese authorities on the victims' status.
"I hope the government, particularly the Foreign Ministry, and the Nepalese authorities will continue efforts to find our loved ones.
"The lack of a definitive answer has left our status in limbo and prevented us from settling various important matters, including insurance claims and asset management," she said.
Fakhrul, 44, better known as Loe, was reported missing in Nepal following devastating floods in the country on Aug 26.
Also reported missing was Malaysian Fire and Rescue Department deputy director of the Fire and Rescue Operations Division, Mohd Sani Harul, who was part of the same climbing expedition.

According to the latest report by the Foreign Ministry (Wisma Putra), 54 Malaysians were still uncontactable, most of whom were believed to have been involved in climbing activities and expeditions in the affected areas.
624c13627424ffc1: KUCHING: A total of 159 residents of a longhouse in the interior of Kapit received food supplies from firefighters after floodwaters submerged its entire ground floor to a depth of more than 2m today.
The 27-door John Kara longhouse in Kerangan was inundated, forcing residents to take shelter on the upper floor for their safety.
A Sarawak Fire and Rescue Department operations centre spokesman said the department received an emergency call about the flooding at 1.30pm.
He said a team from the Kapit Fire and Rescue Station was dispatched to monitor the situation and deliver food supplies to the affected residents.
"An operational team comprising four firefighters arrived at the location at 2.40pm after travelling 68km.
"Upon arrival, the operation commander conducted an initial assessment and confirmed that the entire ground floor of the longhouse had been submerged," he said.
An inspection found that floodwaters had risen to more than 2m on the ground floor, rendering the area uninhabitable.
However, no evacuation or rescue operation was necessary as all residents had already taken shelter on the upper floor.
Firefighters and personnel from other agencies subsequently monitored the situation and distributed food supplies to the affected residents.
After confirming that the situation was safe and under control, the team concluded its operation and returned to the station at 3.07pm.
fa2fcb42dff4b0b8: KUALA LUMPUR: The number of flood evacuees in Perak and Selangor fell to 2,334 people from 683 families this afternoon, down from 2,368 people from 691 families this morning.
The flood situation in Negri Sembilan has also fully recovered, with its last temporary relief centre at SK Jimah closing at 2pm today, according to the Civil Defence Force.
In Perak, the number of evacuees at temporary evacuation centres in five districts dropped to 488 from 499 this morning.
The state Disaster Management Committee secretariat said an evacuation centre at SK Dato' Sagor in Perak Tengah, which housed 22 evacuees, was closed at 3pm today.
However, SK Tanjung Belanja remains open, sheltering 70 evacuees from 35 families.
The number of evacuees at the SRA Rakyat Padang Serai evacuation centre in Manjung remained unchanged at 131, from 39 families.
The Teluk Intan Municipal Council Rest House Hall in Hilir Perak is sheltering 97 evacuees from 31 families, while 10 people from four families remain at SK Batu Hampar in Larut, Matang and Selama.
In Kerian, 180 evacuees from 57 families, including 12 people from three families affected by a landslide, remain at SK Bukit Merah and SK Parit Haji Aman.
In Selangor, the Social Welfare Department's InfoBencana portal reported that the number of evacuees had fallen slightly to 1,846 from 1,869 this morning.

SK Dato' Maharaja Lela is sheltering the highest number of evacuees at 401, followed by SK Parit Mahang (365), SK Sultan Abdul Aziz (222), Sekolah Rendah Agama Bukit Kuching (216), Bukit Kuching Tengah Community Hall (139), SK Rantau Panjang (134) and SRA Batu 8 Ijok (120).

Other centres still operating are SK Jaya Setia, which is sheltering 98 evacuees, Kafa Integrasi Hidayah Bukit Cherakah (66), Seri Harmoni Community Hall (40), SK Batu Arang (25) and Kampung Sungai Kelambu Village Hall (20).
The Malaysian Meteorological Department forecast rain and thunderstorms in some parts of the state this afternoon, with conditions expected to clear by nightfall.
171104ea0ab268b9: KUALA KANGSAR: PKR is not ruling out the possibility of Pakatan Harapan (PH) component parties using their respective logos in the 16th General Election (GE16), saying the proposal warrants consideration by the coalition's top leadership.
Its youth chief Muhammad Kamil Abdul Munim said the proposal should be carefully examined in view of experience from previous elections and the current political landscape.
He said electoral success depended not only on the use of party logos but also on political strategy, track records in public service, engagement with the people and candidate selection.
"I do not deny that there is merit in the proposal and that specific considerations should be taken into account when reviewing our strategies and approaches.

"This matter needs to be examined carefully by the top leadership because winning an election is not just about the logo, but encompasses various aspects, including political strategy, service delivery, our approach to the people and the candidates themselves," he told reporters after the Hari Bertemu Komuniti and Study Assistance Handover programme at the Padang Rengas People's Community Centre.
Kamil was responding to a proposal for PH component parties, including PKR, DAP and Amanah, to use their respective logos in the next general election instead of a single coalition logo.
He said PKR had experience using its own logo in previous elections, which had never caused confusion among voters.
"PKR has been around for almost 30 years and we have seen that there has never been an issue in any election. In fact, we have used the PKR logo before.
"Indeed, the PKR logo made history when it helped PH win the 2018 general election," he said.
51f48c1e9d873edf: LAS VEGAS: Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc voiced frustration after neither driver reached the final top-10 phase of qualifying for Saturday night's Las Vegas Formula One Grand Prix.

Leclerc was 11th fastest and seven-times world champion Hamilton 12th after struggling for straight-line speed down the floodlit Strip on Friday, though both moved up one spot thanks to McLaren's Oscar Piastri taking a 10-place grid drop.
Hamilton said floor damage from debris early in the session had cost him.
"We lost a bunch of downforce with it, a few tenths," the Briton said. "Then we lost this deployment and I lost like six tenths just on deployment.
"When it rains, it pours. That's one of those days."
Leclerc was more critical of the team's execution after making a mistake on what he said was effectively his only meaningful lap.
"For sure, Q3 was possible, but we didn't do a good job," said the Monegasque.
"I made a mistake, and at the same time the execution has been very poor.
"I am very angry now, so I would rather not speak too much, but I think there were plenty of things we could have done much better."
Leclerc said the car's deficit on the long straights would make it difficult to claw back positions in the race.
"Just a very poor qualifying. We are losing a second down the straights, so there's literally nowhere we'll be able to overtake," he added.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen took pole position and will share the front row with Mercedes' George Russell. Newly crowned Formula 1 champion Kimi Antonelli lapped fastest but dropped to sixth due to a grid penalty.
c452b85c2a4bc48e: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose a steep tax on US companies that build data centres overseas.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters at a White House briefing, reported German news agency dpa.
"If they do that, they can. But we're going to put a tremendous tax on them."
It was unclear what authority Trump could use to impose such a tax. Congress sets federal taxes, and Republicans are due to cede control of both chambers to Democrats in January.
Widespread public opposition to data centres in the US helped fuel the Democrats' election victory this month, but Trump has nevertheless remained a staunch supporter of the AI industry.
US companies have been building data centres abroad, including in Europe, for years.
Trump said he wanted more data centres constructed in the US, warning that if they were built abroad, "China will take all of them".
He said the United States was in a race with China to lead in artificial intelligence and argued that the winner would gain a broader advantage.
Trump said he and Chinese President Xi Jinping had agreed on some common safeguards for AI at their meeting this week in Shenzhen but gave no details.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier told CNBC that the two sides had agreed that no major military operation should be launched without human involvement.
ec14581a78d92a2e: SEOUL: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung reiterated on Saturday that the government would offer a reward of 100 million won (US$75,000) to anyone reporting cases of cheating in this week's college entrance examination, describing the misconduct as a "crime as serious as corruption" involving government officials, Yonhap News Agency reported.

Lee made the comments on social media, saying the reward would be paid for each case of cheating reported. This means the total reward could exceed 100 million won if someone reports multiple cases at once.
Lee also said that if a cheater turned themselves in and reported other accomplices, they would receive a reduced punishment for their offence while still receiving the full reward for reporting.

"Cheating on the college entrance exam is a crime as serious as corruption by public officials," Lee said. "We will track cheaters down to the very end and strictly punish exam cheating that steals the lifelong efforts of hundreds of thousands of test-takers."

Offering cash rewards is one of the anti-cheating measures the government has introduced amid growing concerns over the use of artificial intelligence (AI) during national examinations. The concerns followed an admission by this year's top scorer in the certified tax accountant examination that he had cheated with the help of AI and digital devices.

The concerns were further heightened by allegations that a 32-year-old man who scored full marks on the Legal Education Eligibility Test (LEET) had used AI to cheat. The man was found dead at a motel in Seoul on the day of the college entrance examination after failing to attend a live exam session he had promised to take to prove that he had not cheated.

The College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), commonly known as Suneung, marks the culmination of years of rigorous study for many students and is widely regarded as a major life event in South Korea, where university admission can heavily influence career prospects.
ddf15cca3fc941a9: KOTA BHARU: Kelantan police have maintained close cooperation with their Thai counterparts to curb cross-border criminal activities, particularly drug smuggling.
Kelantan police chief Datuk Mohd Yusoff Mamat said the cooperation had helped prevent prohibited substances, especially drugs, from entering the country through the state.
He said Thai authorities had also stepped up border security and planned to establish more checkpoints to tackle cross-border crime.
"We regularly cooperate and maintain contact with the Thai authorities, who have also been tightening security along the border.
"I was informed this morning that they would continue strengthening their border controls and introduce more posts, similar to what we are doing, to address cross-border crime.
"We thank the Thai authorities for helping to arrest drug traffickers and seize drugs before they can be brought into Malaysia, particularly Kelantan," he told reporters here today.
He was speaking after attending the Santai Anak Muda Bikers programme at the Kelantan police contingent headquarters here.

Yusoff also thanked Thai police for foiling a cross-border drug syndicate involving 750kg of methamphetamine, worth an estimated 300 million baht (RM36.3 million), believed to have been destined for Malaysia.
Thai authorities reportedly seized the drugs in Nakhon Si Thammarat province, about 150km north of Hat Yai, at 1.45am (Thai time) on Wednesday.
Two men, aged 31 and 40, were arrested along with a lorry allegedly used to transport the drugs.

The methamphetamine, packed in wrappers bearing the branding of a traditional Chinese tea, was found concealed beneath the lorry's floor panels, which had been modified to create a double-layered compartment.
The drugs were believed to have been transported from Chiang Rai province to Hat Yai district as a transit point before being smuggled into Malaysia.
5162010480fbad9c: KUANTAN: Barisan Nasional (BN) appears to be the most suitable partner for Perikatan Nasional (PN), based on their electoral cooperation in Negri Sembilan and Melaka.
Wawasan secretary-general Datuk Seri Saifuddin Abdullah said the cooperation, dubbed the "Blue Wave", appeared to be gaining traction, particularly in the Negri Sembilan and Melaka state elections.

"There are two levels of cooperation. The first involves partners within the PN coalition, while the second entails political cooperation with any party deemed suitable to help the coalition form the federal government in Putrajaya.
"Based on our experience in Johor, Negri Sembilan and Melaka, BN is currently the most suitable partner," he told reporters after presenting his 2022-2026 parliamentary constituency report card.

Saifuddin said the current arrangement was referred to as the "Blue Wave" or "Muafakat BN-PN", but declined to elaborate, saying any decision on political cooperation would be made by the PN Supreme Council.
He said the council was expected to meet soon to review the outcome of the Negri Sembilan and Melaka state elections and discuss the coalition's future direction.

Asked about the possibility of extending the BN-PN partnership to the 16th general election (GE16), Saifuddin said the broader objective was to work with any party willing to cooperate to form the next federal government.

"This approach (BN-PN) appears to be working well in Negri Sembilan and Melaka. Johor was different, but in Negri Sembilan and Melaka, we adopted the 'Blue Wave' approach, which seems to be effective," he said.

On Nov 15, BN chairman Datuk Seri Dr Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said there were no immediate plans to extend the coalition's cooperation with PN to GE16, although discussions remained possible if circumstances warranted it.
The BN-PN cooperation secured a two-thirds majority in the Negri Sembilan and Melaka state elections.
50848329477db825: PARIS: A French court late on Friday found three police officers involved six years ago in the arrest of Michel Zecler, a Black music producer, guilty of beating him up with racist intent and falsifying the subsequent police report.
The men were sentenced to prison terms ranging from one year under electronic monitoring to two years in custody with all of them banned from working in the police force again.
Zecler's legal team had asked the court to consider the racial nature of the attack, which was upheld by the court.
The police officers had put together a false report accusing Zecler of assaulting them and filed a complaint against him for resisting arrest.
"Justice has been done. It restores a man's dignity and, at the same time, allows him to begin rebuilding his life," Zecler's lawyer Serge Money told Franceinfo radio.
The assault came to light after closed-circuit television and mobile phone footage circulated online showing the men beating up the producer.
b89c49e91e814bb0: SEREMBAN: The Negri Sembilan Department of Wildlife and National Parks (Perhilitan) will install camera traps to detect a black panther after residents reported sightings in the Laman Sendayan residential area.
Its director, Wan Mat Wan Harun, said the move is to verify the complaint's authenticity before taking further action.

"We received the report around 2pm today, and our team will set up camera traps this evening," he told Bernama here today.

Earlier today, several photos uploaded by users on social media went viral, showing the animal roaming around, believed to be searching for food in the area.
dd423078e31c333f: IPOH: A 13-year-old Malay College Kuala Kangsar (MCKK) student who was reported missing yesterday was found safe in Taiping, four hours after police received a report on the disappearance.
Kuala Kangsar police chief Assistant Commissioner Heisham Harun said police received a report from the student's mother around 6pm after she was informed by the school that her child was missing.
He said police launched a search with the assistance of the Perak Criminal Investigation Department's Tracker Dog Unit (K9), as well as the school and family members.

"Following information provided by the public, the student was successfully located by the police in the Taiping district around 10pm and has been reunited with their parents in good and safe condition," he said in a statement.
Heisham said the incident was not connected, directly or indirectly, to the death of another student which was reported last Wednesday.
Earlier, a post went viral on social media about a Form One student from a boarding school in Kuala Kangsar who had been missing since yesterday.
a182c69847a4c110: HANYU: Tens of thousands of mascot fans gathered in a city near Tokyo on Saturday to meet and greet more than 200 life-size cuddly characters that promote local towns and businesses.
In the land of Hello Kitty and Pokemon, mascots are used to promote everything from prison to railways to private businesses, and popular ones gain full-on celebrity status.
"This is the first time I've ever come to an event like this, so I'm kind of excited," Yuriko Okamori, 51, told AFP at the annual meetup event.
The mascot meetup has been held in the city of Hanyu since 2010 and nearly 220 mascots were invited to join this year, according to organisers.
On a stage, a troupe of animal mascots danced to upbeat pop music as a large crowd filmed them on smartphones and clapped along.

Elsewhere, a popular pony mascot representing Gunma prefecture was surrounded by fans eager for selfies, while a cat mascot was pushed through the packed crowd on a cart to make its way across the venue.
City official Shogo Dei, who oversees the event, said 80,000 people attended the two-day meetup last year and that organisers expect a similar turnout this year.
"These local mascot characters representing regions are part of Japanese culture. Our aim is to help revitalize towns across Japan through these characters," Dei told AFP.
Mascots in Japan can generate millions of dollars in revenue if they become successful, even without the global recognition of major intellectual property brands such as Pikachu.

Another popular character, Hikonyan, a samurai helmet-wearing cat mascot associated with Hikone Castle in western Japan, has helped draw tourists to the area. The character even received around 10,000 New Year's greeting cards from across Japan this January.
"There are so many different characters representing different places, and it's not uncommon to see even adults carrying mascot goods on their bags," Okamori said.
b9c9ff69359939a4: KUALA LUMPUR: The Sultan of Pahang, Al-Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah, has reminded graduates not to become a generation that excels in lecture halls but fails in moral character.
The ruler said knowledge should be used to build the nation and unite society, rather than undermine unity and fuel hostility.

Al-Sultan Abdullah also reminded the younger generation and the public not to become so arrogant that they casually questioned the foundations of the nation that had long safeguarded the people's way of life.
"Do not let opportunities, space and freedom go to your head, causing you to forget your roots as you rise higher.

"Indeed, freedom is not a licence to act as one pleases. Courage is no excuse for being rude, and wisdom is not measured by how loudly one goes against the tide or questions everything without a basis in knowledge and facts," he said.
He was speaking at the 23rd convocation ceremony of Universiti Kuala Lumpur (UniKL) at the Kuala Lumpur World Trade Centre here.
Al-Sultan Abdullah said not everyone who went against the tide was a fighter, not everyone who spoke loudly was right, and not everyone who was fond of questioning things was wise.

"We have never rejected differences of opinion or constructive criticism, but criticism must be based on facts, advice must be given with courtesy, and differences in stance must not lead to a loss of judgement," he said.
Also in attendance were Tengku Ampuan Pahang Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah and Tengku Mahkota Pahang Tengku Hassanal Ibrahim Alam Shah.
Among those accompanying them were deputy prime minister and UniKL pro-chancellor Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, UniKL vice-chancellor Prof Kushsairy Abdul Kadir and Mara chairman Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki.

ae5c20d896cc5583: IPOH: Police detained four teenagers, all under 15, for allegedly obstructing public servants from performing their duties at Km286.5 of the North-South Expressway northbound, near Simpang Pulai, yesterday.

Tapah deputy police chief deputy superintendent Mohd Fadzil Ismail said a team of policemen on patrol received information at 4.20pm from the district police headquarters control centre to assist Ringlet station personnel in tracking down a Toyota Chery multi-purpose vehicle occupied by several people suspected of being involved in a kidnapping case.
He said policemen then moved to Batu 3, Jalan Pahang, near Tapah, to conduct surveillance and spotted the vehicle about 5.30pm.
"Police instructed the driver to stop for inspection, but the driver failed to comply and instead sped off, nearly hitting an on-duty policeman.
"Police then chased the vehicle to the Tapah toll plaza. In an attempt to intercept it, the police vehicle's bumper was hit by the suspect's vehicle," he said in a statement today.
Fadzil said personnel from the Ipoh district police headquarters joined the chase before police intercepted the vehicle at Simpang Pulai.
He said all four suspects were arrested and the vehicle seized.
Initial investigations found that all four were teenagers, while urine screening tests showed they were drug-free and had no criminal records, he added.
"The three boys detained have been remanded for four days from today, while the girl was granted police bail as she is involved in an ongoing investigation in Jitra, Kedah," he said.
The case is being investigated under Sections 186, 279 and 353 of the Penal Code.
7d406da7a274afdf: SHAH ALAM: A surge of up to 25 per cent above the daily average in patients seeking treatment at the Yellow Zone of Ampang Hospital's Emergency and Trauma Department has caused congestion and prolonged waiting times for ward admission.
The Selangor Health Department said the recent increase in patient numbers had also affected the smooth processing of admissions to the hospital's wards.
"The Emergency and Trauma Department at Ampang Hospital has seen a significant increase in patients at its Yellow Zone recently, with numbers rising by up to 25 per cent above the daily average.
"This has caused congestion at the department and affected the time taken for patients to be admitted to wards," it said in a statement.
The department said Ampang Hospital's management introduced several measures to address the congestion following the surge in patients.
This includes strengthening patient admission and discharge processes to ensure smoother patient flow.
"Additionally, the use of the discharge lounge has been expanded to improve efficiency, while ensuring human resource management is carried out effectively.
"The department appreciates public feedback and remains committed to ensuring optimal healthcare delivery without compromising patient safety and treatment management," it said.
It was reported that congestion at the hospital's Emergency Department, particularly the Yellow Zone, had left patients requiring further treatment waiting longer for ward beds.
Threads user @ayien78 claimed that almost every available space in the zone was occupied by beds and mobile beds to accommodate patients.
She also claimed that her father had been waiting for three days to be admitted to a ward but had yet to secure a bed due to overcrowding.
The situation not only left elderly patients waiting for extended periods but also placed a heavy burden on healthcare workers dealing with the high patient volume.
f4086de407ae83df: BEIJING: Donald Trump hailed the fanfare of his meeting this week with Xi Jinping as a victory, but the US president has gained little from three such summits this year while the Chinese leader has strengthened his position on the world stage, analysts say.

Xi emerged from a global gathering in China as a statesman who could convene the first China-US-Russia summit and he keeps a fragile trade truce with the US in a holding pattern — where Beijing likes it — even as Washington takes a harder line.
At least in terms of public announcements, Trump has few concrete gains to show.

"They have achieved the Chinese Communist Party's and Xi's goal, which was to keep dragging things out and keep talking," said Kuo Yu-jen, director of Taiwan's National Sun Yat-sen University's Institute of China and Asia-Pacific Studies.
Trump-XI summits gives China 'strategic space'

Xi broke with protocol to greet Trump at Shenzhen airport ahead of Thursday's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit. Trump called the gesture "a big win" even before his meetings began, similar to how he has described the pomp of previous meetings.
Xi orchestrated moments befitting a visiting president focused on legacy-building: the pair shared a hug at the airport and held the first-ever trilateral meeting with Russia's Vladimir Putin.
On substance, Xi was less generous.

Trump told media outlets he and his Chinese counterpart had spoken about AI, trade and oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz. The US demands Beijing buy more US farm goods, ease curbs on rare-earth minerals vital to key industries and release two Americans who Washington says are wrongfully detained.

China's Foreign Ministry said the two sides agreed to map out an action plan for building a "constructive relationship of strategic stability" — a framework already unveiled in May. The ministry gave no details or timeline.

Beijing's readout did not mention the fragile US-China trade truce, China's agricultural commitments, rare earths, chip controls, the scandal over US chip giant Nvidia or the detained Americans, and did not name Iran.

China is on track to meet its soybean pledge for 2026 but has delivered only a fraction of the other promised farm purchases, while rare-earth shipments remain far below the levels before the trade war escalated last year, and neither detained American has been freed.

Xi also pushed his key demand that the US "keep doing the right thing" on Taiwan or risk setbacks in the bilateral relationship, according to the ministry. China views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, a claim Taipei rejects.

"China has secured additional strategic space, including the US stance on the Taiwan issue and the easing of the technology embargo. Strategically, the US has indeed gained nothing," said Dan Wang, China director at the Eurasia Group think tank.
Trump's agenda focused heavily on the meeting with Xi and Putin, which released a joint "Declaration Toward Peace" that analysts described as vague.
Hosting the trilateral summit, which Trump had pushed for, offered Xi a platform to cast himself as a central player in managing global affairs, analysts said.
China bides its time as US gets tougher on chips

Since this month's resignation of Jensen Huang, a Trump ally, as Nvidia's CEO over the revelation that he had had an affair with a woman who US intelligence believes is a Chinese spy, the Trump administration has sought to close loopholes that let Chinese companies bypass US restrictions on AI chip exports.

On the day Trump and Xi met, a US rule further restricting China's access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia took effect. The US administration is also weighing a rule requiring US companies to disclose their use of Chinese AI models.
US lawmakers have also been moving against China.

Beijing, which seeks to encourage Trump to stabilise bilateral relations while defending Chinese industries, has vowed retaliation against such curbs and is in no hurry to meet US demands, analysts say.

"The Chinese see these noises as a natural part of the relationship," said Shen Weizhong, a former Chinese Foreign Ministry official who now works for Beijing-based think tank Global Governance Institution.
"The Chinese have learned their lesson: they won't fulfil their side of a promise all at once. They'll do it step by step," he said.
Holding back concessions gives Beijing leverage if Washington adopts a tougher stance, as pressure builds in Congress from lawmakers in both parties.

This week, a House of Representatives committee report called for restricting investment in China's aerospace sector and a senator introduced legislation to revoke China's normal trade status and favourable tariff treatment.

An extension of the trade truce is expected to wait until a meeting of Group of 20 leaders in Miami next month, when Xi and Trump are expected to meet again. The truce, struck at a meeting in South Korea last year and extended during Xi's visit to Washington in September, expires on Jan 10.

The "low-hanging fruits have been harvested" after extensive trade talks over the past year, said Even Rogers Pay, director at Beijing-based consultancy Trivium China. "It may feel like a holding pattern by comparison to past summits, but in the current context it's actually a significant step, given the recent midterm elections and the Jensen Huang scandal."
Analysts expect the year's fourth Trump-Xi meeting will also be heavy on optics.
"But substantially, I don't think there's going to be very big progress. It's going to be about stability and stability," said Shen, the Chinese former official. "And that's enough."

fff46e9ea2cb1a6a: KUALA LUMPUR: MCA Youth has called on the government to revive local elections, starting with the federal territories.

The wing’s chief, Ling Tian Soon, said local council elections in the federal territories will provide residents with the opportunity to elect representatives, similar to how those in other states vote for assemblymen.
The federal territories of Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya and Labuan do not have state legislative assembly seats.
“Those who live in Kuala Lumpur can only vote for an MP.
“So we propose for the federal government to revive local council elections,” Ling told reporters after the MCA Youth general assembly here today.

Local elections were held in the past before being suspended in 1965 - after a state of emergency was declared because of the Indonesia-Malaysia Confrontation - and effectively abolished a year later.

Last year, federal territories DAP chief Tan Kok Wai called for the restoration of local elections following the abrupt departure of Kuala Lumpur mayor Maimunah Sharif a little over a year after being appointed.

In August, a feasibility report on amending the Federal Capital Act 1960 said that reviving local elections could conflict with the Federal Territory of Kuala Lumpur Agreement 1974, which formed the basis for Kuala Lumpur’s establishment as a federal territory.

Ling also said MCA Youth is urging the government to reinstate a National Higher Education Fund Corporation (PTPTN) loan repayment exemption policy for graduates of private higher education institutions who earned first-class honours degrees.
He said that many borrowers relied on such loans as they came from low and middle income households.
“We want the government to reinstate the initiative to be fair to this group of students,” he said.

Under the 2026 budget, the government introduced a targeted PTPTN loan repayment exemption for first-class honours graduates from public universities, limited to students from the B40 and M40 income groups.

Higher education minister Zambry Abdul Kadir said last year the suspension of the loan waiver for students from private universities was to allow the ministry to reassess the definition of “first class” across both public and private universities to ensure fairness.
19b754834fc05f4c: PETALING JAYA: Gabungan Rakyat Sabah (GRS) has yet to decide on the political cooperation for the 16th general election (GE16), says secretary-general Armizan Mohd Ali.

He said any decision must take into account the views of component parties as they reflect the voices of members at the grassroots level as well as the signals sent by the public during the 2025 Sabah state election.

"Regarding the core issues and policies on cooperation and political direction, my personal views are not what matters, what is important are the deliberations and decisions made collectively by the leadership through the GRS supreme council," Bernama quoted him as telling reporters after officiating the "Disaster Preparedness: Amateur Radio as Alternative Communication" programme (Sabah state level) here.

Armizan, who is also the domestic trade and cost of living minister, said GRS had yet to hold any discussion with other political parties on their possible cooperation in GE16. Instead, the coalition is currently focussed on strengthening its position across all constituencies.

He said establishing a stable government at both the federal and state levels to ensure smooth administration and the effective delivery of services to the people would be a key factor in determining the coalition's political direction.

He made these remarks when asked to comment on a proposal for GRS to cooperate with Barisan Nasional (BN) under the Muafakat Sabah framework, a suggestion recently raised by Tenom Umno chief Raime Unggi, as well as the possibility of continuing the existing cooperation with Pakatan Harapan (PH).
Armizan said every political party has the right to determine its own direction heading into an election, and he does not want to comment on the stances taken by other parties.
However, he said GRS is open to political cooperation to ensure the stability of the state administration.

He said the coalition's previous experiences with political cooperation, alongside feedback from component party members and signals from voters in the Sabah state election, would be key factors to consider before a collective decision is made on its direction for GE16.
c3204e64766474b7: KUALA LUMPUR: Datuk Richard Scully wants the Football Coaches Association of Malaysia (FCAM) presidency to be a full-time role, saying the association needs dedicated leadership to tackle long-standing issues facing coaches.

The former National Football Development Programme (NFDP) head of coach education is seeking the post on a platform focused on protecting coaches' welfare, expanding development opportunities and strengthening FCAM's voice in Malaysian football.
"I believe the FCAM president's position should be full-time because of the important role it plays in Malaysian football," said Richard.
"We have seen plenty of issues faced by Malaysian football coaches. We need to be a strong voice in the local football ecosystem."

Richard, who is challenging incumbent Datuk Ong Kim Swee and former international Azlan Johar in the Nov 28 election, said unpaid wages remained one of the biggest concerns, with salary arrears recurring every season.
"We need to be proactive in helping our members. So many coaches face unpaid wages, and this happens season after season. We must ensure their welfare is properly taken care of," he said.
Beyond welfare concerns, Scully wants FCAM to broaden its reach beyond the M-League by providing greater support to academy and grassroots coaches.
"There are many academy coaches who need guidance. FCAM can help them improve and move up the coaching pyramid," he added.

Among his key proposals are stronger job security, fairer remuneration and better contractual protection, alongside wider opportunities for coaches to obtain licences and upgrade their qualifications.
He also wants FCAM to organise more regular coaching courses, seminars and refresher programmes while working towards standardised training modules and clearer development pathways.

For women coaches, Richard has outlined a five-pillar plan that includes a scholarship fund to subsidise between 50 and 100 per cent of AFC C, B and A coaching licence fees in collaboration with the Football Association of Malaysia (FAM).
The plan also features mentorship programmes, international exposure and efforts to secure paid professional contracts for women coaches with state teams and academies.

Another initiative aims to improve access to head coaching roles, with qualified women coaches who have served one to two years as assistants guaranteed an interview or given priority consideration when vacancies arise.

FCAM members will elect their leadership for the next term at the association's annual congress on Nov 28. Kim Swee, who won unopposed in November 2023, faces his first contested presidential race since taking office.
43ae2a9b2e908669: KUALA LUMPUR: SM Muthu could be heading back into Malaysian athletics administration, with Selangor’s new leadership expected to lift lifetime bans on him and four other former officials at its first executive council meeting tomorrow.

The move would end their exclusion from the affairs of the Selangor Athletics Association (SAA) and could pave the way for Muthu to rejoin the Malaysia Athletics (MA) executive council as Selangor’s representative.
Sources familiar with the new administration’s plans identified the five officials as Muthu, K Pregash, R Murugan, G Mohan and S Gunaseelan.
Fauzi Nanivanan Abdullah of Hulu Selangor, the sixth official originally banned, is not included in the proposed move and is expected to remain suspended.
The new executive council is also expected to appoint Muthu chairman of SAA’s disciplinary committee. Members will confirm the appointment at tomorrow’s meeting.
The post could provide a route back to the national federation’s executive council, subject to the necessary formalities with MA. SAA will also notify the sports commissioner of its decisions.
The anticipated changes follow the election of a new SAA leadership earlier this month, when Muthu’s son Ganesh defeated incumbent Nurhayati Karim 15-9 to win the presidency.
Nurhayati’s team lost almost every contest, with former DAP MP Ong Kian Ming the sole exception. He won the deputy presidency unopposed.
Lifting the bans would reverse one of the most divisive episodes in the association’s recent history.
SAA imposed lifetime suspensions on the six officials in June 2025 after they challenged the legitimacy of the association’s annual general meeting (AGM) on April 26 that year.
They later convened an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) on June 9, which declared the earlier AGM null and void.

The then SAA leadership refused to recognise the EGM. It subsequently banned the six under Articles 13.5, 13.6 and 13.7 of the association’s constitution, which cover disciplinary action and the authority of the main committee.
The officials represented six district affiliates: Petaling, Hulu Langat, Kuala Langat, Sepang, Klang and Hulu Selangor. Their suspensions did not remove them from their district posts.
They remained office bearers but could no longer take part in SAA affairs. Muthu, for example, continued as president of the Petaling district association.

Muthu’s expected appointment as disciplinary committee chairman carries particular significance. He previously led both SAA and MA, and the new role could put him back in a position to represent Selangor at the national level.

However, lifting the bans alone will not resolve the dispute that fractured the state association. The new administration will need to explain why it considers the reversals justified and how it plans to address the divisions that led to the sanctions.
Hulu Selangor’s position also remains unresolved. The district sat out the recent SAA election because of internal problems, and Fauzi’s continued suspension leaves it outside the proposed move.
Tomorrow’s meeting should offer the first clear indication of how the new leadership intends to handle the bans and whether it is ready to reshape the association’s administration.
For Muthu, the proposed appointment could mark a return to the heart of athletics administration after years of exclusion from the state body’s affairs.
For SAA, the bigger test will be whether the changes can restore confidence and end a prolonged period of division.
2f07812ae521d022: KUALA LUMPUR: A Malaysian man was arrested after attempting to smuggle 4kgs of gold worth about RM2.25 million hidden in his shoes at the Minangkabau International Airport in Padang, Indonesia.
The 34-year-old was detained at the departure area while preparing to board a flight to Malaysia on Nov 12.
Teluk Bayur Customs Office chief Ade Zirwan said the inspection was conducted with the assistance of airport security personnel.
"During monitoring, we received information about a passenger who was behaving suspiciously.

"Following this, officers carried out further surveillance and analysis before inspecting the passenger," he said in a statement published on the Indonesian Directorate General of Customs and Excise website.
Ade said the inspection uncovered four gold bars hidden in the man's shoes, with two bars concealed in each shoe.
He said tests using specialised detection equipment confirmed that the gold had a purity of more than 99 per cent and weighed about 4kgs in total.
"The gold was not declared to customs as required under regulations governing goods taken out of Indonesia.
"It also violated restrictions and prohibitions on goods being taken out of the country," he said.
He said the gold was estimated to be worth 10 billion rupiah (about RM2.25 million).
The man is being investigated under Section 102A of Law No. 17 of 2006 on Customs, which carries a jail term of between one and 10 years upon conviction.
The provision also carries a fine of between 50 million rupiah (about RM11,250) and five billion rupiah (about RM1.13 million).
"The suspect is currently being held for 20 days at the West Sumatra Regional Police detention centre, while all evidence has been seized for further legal action.
"We are also working with the West Sumatra Regional Police and Padang Pariaman Police to complete the investigation," he said.
46d27f41b524d795: KUALA LUMPUR: The Education Ministry (MOE) is looking into the need to increase the number of assistant wardens and guidance and counselling teachers to ensure students receive optimal attention and support while staying in hostels.

Its minister, Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek, said the aspiration of parents to see their children gain admission to fully residential schools should be balanced with the children's own abilities and emotional readiness.

"As we plan for our children's future, it is important that we also listen to their voices and understand their feelings. Our dreams as parents must align with our children's own abilities and emotional readiness," she said in a Facebook post today.

Fadhlina said that she had held discussions with the police in Kuala Kangsar, Perak, on strengthening the safety and well-being of students residing in the hostel of the educational institution concerned.

The discussions covered compliance with standard operating procedures (SOPs), hostel management, and the importance of parents assessing their children's level of readiness before sending them to boarding schools.

She said every child had a different level of adaptability, with some adjusting quickly while others required more time, adding that some children were able to cope well with academic competition, while others needed greater encouragement.
As such, she said it was important to create an environment where children could share their thoughts and be heard without being judged.
"I want parents to know that we share the same hopes. We want our children to succeed, but more importantly, we want them to grow up safe and happy," she added.
She also advised parents not to be overly concerned if their children do not gain admission to their dream schools, as every child has his or her own unique path and timeline for achieving success.
"Most importantly, regardless of where they study, they must know that our love and acceptance never depend on the name of their school or their examination results," she added.

Khasab lies on Oman's Musandam Peninsula at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway that carried nearly one-fifth of global crude oil supplies before the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.
Shipping through the strait has been disrupted since Iran moved to close the waterway following the eruption of the conflict on Feb 28.

a18ebd94743425b3: JOHOR BARU: A family escaped injury after a car crashed into a power pole outside their home in Bandar Permas Jaya here, causing the pole to fall onto the roof and damage part of the house.
The 71-year-old homeowner, Ab Manaf Sujak, said he shuddered at the thought of what could have happened had the pole landed on the bedroom where his family was sleeping.
"I cannot imagine what would have happened to my family if the power pole had fallen on the bedroom," he said.
The chicken rice seller said his family was asleep when the incident occurred about 2am today. He woke up after hearing a loud crash and went outside to investigate.
"I was shocked to find the more than 5m-tall power pole had fallen onto the roof, damaging part of it. It also struck the boundary wall, a canopy beside the house and the front of a car.
"I also saw a car in the drain. Without hesitation, I went over and found that the driver was safe.
"The driver, who was in his 20s, claimed to have lost control of the car before crashing into the power pole and ending up in the drain," he said when contacted.
Ab Manaf said he was grateful that his 65-year-old wife and 20-year-old grandson, who were also at home, were unharmed.
"There have been several incidents of cars skidding into the drain in this area, but this is the first time one has caused damage to a house.
"I am at a loss over how to cover the cost of repairing the damage caused by the driver's negligence.
"The driver's family has met us and apologised for the incident.
"However, we are unsure whether they will bear the repair costs," he said.
Ab Manaf said he had lodged a report at the Johor Bahru Selatan District Traffic Police Station.

ddf0ef30b2b30e12: JOHANNESBURG: Tributes poured in on Saturday for South Africa's former deputy president and head of UN Women, Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, who has died at the age of 71.

She "believed that gender equality is not a favour to be granted but a right to be claimed", he said.
In an interview with SABC, UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed recalled Mlambo-Ngcuka's interventions on behalf of women and girls in Afghanistan, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Nigeria.
"She pushed the limits and I think that that's where we got a lot of the confidence to do the things that we do, following in her footsteps," she said.

In a statement on X, Mohammed said Mlambo-Ngcuka "fought for women's leadership till the end", including by calling for a woman to succeed Guterres as secretary-general after his second term ends on Dec 31.

20995ab28558b3eb: NEW DELHI: At least 11 people have died and more than 180 have been hospitalised after drinking suspected tainted alcohol in India's northeastern state of Manipur.
The victims fell ill after consuming the liquor, Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh said in a statement on Friday.

He also ordered an enquiry into the incident, saying those responsible would be arrested and punished.
Deaths from illicit or adulterated alcohol are regularly reported in India, where cheap liquor sold outside regulated channels can contain methanol, a highly toxic industrial chemical.
In May, at least 15 people died after drinking methanol-laced illicit liquor in Pune and neighbouring Pimpri-Chinchwad in the western state of Maharashtra.

56b4c092930898f6: It's been a bad few weeks for technology on and off the planet, as NASA reported problems with its Perseverance Mars rover and Odyssey orbiter this week.

For Perseverance, the problem seems to be a relatively straightforward communications issue that has paused science operations because of low data rates. The Odyssey orbiter, however, is facing an issue that could end the mission.

The 2001 Mars Odyssey reached orbit around Mars in October 2001 to search for evidence of water and ice on the surface. The mission was supposed to last two and a half years, but the spacecraft's operations have been extended for a quarter of a century.

In that time, it has had its fair share of ups and downs, including the failure of one of its four reaction wheels in 2013. Three reaction wheels are needed to orient the spacecraft; otherwise, it must fall back to its hydrazine thrusters.

Earlier in November, between the 4th and 6th, Odyssey dropped into safe mode, which engineers determined was caused by one of the remaining reaction wheels stopping spinning. Science data stopped flowing as the team worked to recover the component; the good news was that the wheel moved when commanded. The bad news is that if the thrusters need to be used, only a few months of fuel remain.

More bad news is that the spacecraft is part of NASA's Mars Relay Network, and was responsible for sending back the first post-landing images from the Phoenix lander and the Spirit, Opportunity, and Curiosity rovers. Its loss (should it come to that) would therefore be keenly felt.

In the event the orbiter is indeed approaching the end of the road, the European Space Agency's Mars Express (MEX) and Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) could pick up some of the load although, as a former ESA insider put it: "MEX is a science mission that can do relay where TGO is a relay mission that also does science." According to NASA, TGO already sends the most relay data from Mars to Earth.

The challenge facing the Perseverance trundlebot is one of communication. On October 30, the rover's main computer detected problems with the primary radio (a series of "heartbeats" from the device did not arrive as expected) and automatically switched to a redundant backup, placing itself in a protective safe mode.

So far, so expected. Engineers brought the rover back from safe mode, analyzed the data, and made an unpleasant discovery. The backup radio was not performing as it should – it was operating at approximately half of its expected power output.

Both radios were therefore deemed inoperable – at least until the team has got to the bottom of the issues – and the rover has used X-band communications over its high-gain antenna to talk to Earth ever since. The problem here is that the connection provides a significantly lower data rate, meaning science and instrument operations are on hold.
Engineers are working first to return the backup radio to operational status, then to address the primary. ®
a7c90dfb0b90f09c: ANTALYA: The COP31 climate talks spilled into Saturday as countries raced to secure a deal after a draft text dropped all mention of fossil fuels, exposing deep divisions over how to tackle global warming.

Nearly 200 nations remained deadlocked after two weeks of grinding UN talks in Turkey, with negotiators working through the night after missing their scheduled Friday finish amid feuds over energy, science and finance.
Australia, which is presiding over the COP31 negotiations, raced against the clock to produce a third draft deal, with many delegates due to catch flights home.
"We are close to the finish line, but we are not there yet," COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is Turkey's environment minister, told an assembly late Friday that approved some technical matters.
Midway through his opening address, Kurum was forced to pause while a protester shouted "You are killing the future!" before being escorted from the hall.
Expectations of a major breakthrough have been low at COP31 as countries grapple with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions stemming from the war in Iran.
The summit follows a string of climate-linked disasters from Europe to Nepal and Indonesia and unfolds as a super El Nino pattern amplifies the risk of further extreme weather.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, a flashpoint at UN climate talks where producers such as Saudi Arabia have fiercely resisted such calls.
A second, pared-down draft released on Thursday stripped away all mentions of fossil fuels -- sending negotiators rushing back to the bargaining table.
The European Union said the revised draft "risks turning this climate COP into a fossil summit".
A dozen European and developing countries -- from France to Panama and the Solomon Islands -- released a letter Friday insisting that the deal include "a clear transition away from fossil fuels".

Panama, which also signed the letter, threatened to walk away from the talks. The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, is a vocal critic of the climate negotiations, accusing a "petroleum mafia" of blocking progress.

Meanwhile, the OPEC oil cartel wrote on X that its head, Haitham Al Ghais, met Russian presidential climate envoy Ruslan Edelgeriev at COP31 to discuss "the importance of inclusive and balanced approaches across all multilateral environmental fora".
Clean electrification
Australia's Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who shuttled between delegations to seek compromises, said Friday he would work "for as long as it takes, to get the job done".

The draft "cover decision" proposes a target to electrify the global economy -- a push to replace technologies that burn fossil fuels directly, like diesel cars and gas heating, with electric alternatives.

The goal is championed by COP31 hosts Turkey and Australia, who tout "electrification" as integral to tackling concerns over energy security and sluggish global progress in cutting heat-trapping emissions.
"Electrification is the key to transitioning away from fossil fuels," said Bowen, who is chairing the negotiations.
The proposal calls for countries to boost the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035.
But it does not specify that the additional electricity must come from renewables rather than coal or gas, spurring some countries to demand an explicitly "clean" target.
Some countries also rejected a proposal to ramp up carbon capture, dismissing it as a costly, unproven technology that could allow polluters to keep burning fossil fuels.
US$120 billion target
Countries are sharply divided over a raft of other issues.
The timing of the next set of reports by the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has been a major source of friction.
The latest draft expressed "deep concern" over the imminent breach of the 1.5C goal but dropped an earlier call to return warming below that threshold as soon as possible this century.
Negotiations are also deadlocked over long-running complaints by developing countries that rich nations are falling short in their obligations to help them confront climate change.
The removal of a US$120 billion target for climate adaptation angered developing nations.
"We didn't come here to beg," said Ghana's environment minister, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings.

4d98effdc3566e59: The dominant Nepali food narrative overlooks the diverse regional histories and culinary traditions of Indigenous communities
Originally published on Global Voices
Timu khole, wild mushroom soup. Photo by Binti Gurung. Used with permission.

Food enriches our soul. It makes us who we are. However, the emergence of cosmopolitanism and global and local food politics has sidelined Indigenous food, not to mention the traditions and rituals associated with them.

“Over the last decades, ever since the country was opened up to the outside world in the 1950s, in search of a national food identity, the staple daal bhaat, a nutrient-dense combination of lentils and rice accompanied by vegetables, has been elevated to Nepal’s national dish,” writes Binti Gurung, a food historian and founder of Natural Roots Foundation, an organization dedicated to documenting, preserving, and promoting Indigenous Himalayan food heritage, traditional recipes, and local knowledge in Nepal. “The national food narrative that is being set completely obscures the varied regional histories and food practices of the Indigenous peoples.”
The Foundation, established in 2017, promotes the many varieties of food that have become neglected in Nepal, especially the plants and herbs that can be foraged in the forests and mountains.

Working with Aama Samuha, a collective of women’s groups set up to maintain cultural traditions and support communal activities in Nepali villages, she has been documenting and archiving the food knowledge primarily held by Indigenous women in Nepal.

The Lekhali Cookbook, authored by Gurung, draws its name from lekh, the high ridges in Nepal, and highlights the rich food tradition shared by women’s groups from Nepal’s Mustang, Manang, Lamjung, and Gorkha districts.
Sanjib Chaudhary of Global Voices caught up with Binti Gurung to talk about her work on food heritage. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Sanjib Chaudhary (SC): Can you introduce yourself and tell us a bit about your work?

Binti Gurung (BG): Before talking about the food heritage of Nepal, it’s necessary to mention that knowing the broader political and historical context of the country is important because a lot of what my work looks into connects with understanding of the past.

The pivotal moment can be attributed to the 1950s, when the absolutist regime came to an end. As a country, Nepal had remained closed off to the outside world for so long that very little was understood about Nepali society, particularly its food practices.

Within this environment of reaching out to the past events that happened in this land, uncovering the stories of the people, and mainly breaking down and deconstructing the idea of “Nepali-ness,” lies the understanding of our food heritage.

I myself come from what used to be called a Gurung country until the 1970s. I know something about our collective history as Gurung people, and that my great-grandfather on the maternal side was a mukhiya, a tribal chief somewhere in that Gurung country. There are no written documents about our lineage, apart from the knowledge that remains in the tongue. I take pride in that, but it also means some knowledge has not been transmitted.

My paternal grandfather was the first person to be educated because of his connection to British India, after which he did a lot in his village, which included donating some of his personal land to the village school. Whereas I am the first in my family to go to university, learn English (like the rest of my generation), and read history.
SC: Food sovereignty is a burning issue for Indigenous peoples. Can you give us an overview of what challenges Indigenous communities in Nepal are facing with regard to food sovereignty?

BG: Even though the constitution of 2015 has given recognition to the right to food, how does it translate to the many Indigenous groups accessing their food? Are the Indigenous peoples who have been living by the rivers and the forests able to access the foods that they have learned to process, collect, and eat?

For the communities that still live in or near the forest, how are their relationships affected when forests are turned into national parks? Do the Indigenous peoples who have been relying on these ancestral food practices have access? Can the state recognize and permit it?
When we start to think this way, we go beyond the conversation about food sovereignty because then we have to talk about the land and the peoples who inhabit it, and their connection to it.
The author in conversation with women's group members. Photo via Binti Gurung. Used with permission.

SC: Nepal is a multi-ethnic country, and communities have their own food and agriculture systems. However, food politics is prevalent, with some communities claiming a particular dish as solely theirs. What’s your take on this?

BG: I think it is impossible to claim any particular dish as solely belonging to only one community. After all, we live in a shared world. We are beings in constant interaction with the land. Like any living practice that is evolving, our food practices are also in motion; it is not a static, fixed thing.

What may be helpful is to think about how a dish or food practice evolved. Or even to try to understand how it has evolved the way it has, including the factors of influence. Even though we think of Nepali communities having their own food systems, if we look underneath somewhere, we can find some similar practices.

One example is the way food is harvested from the forest; this particular practice, whether in the high mountains, hills, or the Terai, remains similar. Of course, how this practice is treated by those not practicing is an entirely different thing.

SC: It’s high time we promote Indigenous food in a global space. Can you tell us about your recent book “The Lekhali Cookbook: Indigenous Food Heritage from the Highlands of Nepal” and the dishes you’d like to share with a wider audience?

BG: This book has been in the making for a very long time. When I started doing this work in 2017, at some point it felt very urgent to understand the issues around it, and gradually it became important to start documenting in a written way because a lot had been unknown.
The cover of The Lekhali Cookbook. Photo by Sanjib Chaudhary. Used with permission.

There may be many factors why the conversation around food heritage has remained so obscure, but one that I attribute strongly to is our own political history that has shaped the Indigenous experiences.

For many Indigenous communities, the problem has also been due to others writing about their history. Of course, there are some very rare scholars who have done a fine job, but in the case of our own history, there is now an immense effort to establish or re-establish our origin account. It’s very saddening to have to read about some of these accounts. And then there is also the process of verifying and fact-checking, and that takes a lot of time.

The Lekhali Cookbook came into being due to a generous grant from the British Council. A lot of the work had been conducted prior to receiving the grant, but it allowed us to visit the villages in the central Himalayas and work with aama samuha [translated as “mothers’ groups,” acting as local women’s collectives] who are heavily involved in the food production process. Based on the consultation with the groups, we collected the recipes of the eight villages of Lamjung, Manang, Mustang, and Gorkha.

In the book, we have some unique recipes that many people do not know, such as the foraged panyu (wild rhubarb), kru (yak sausage), yak curry with satu, or farsi ko bhat eaten with sattu up in the high Gorkha hills.
SC: What do you think the future of Indigenous food will look like in a decade's time? What should Indigenous communities, in your opinion, do to preserve and promote their food heritage?

BG: I think we have immense challenges ahead of us. Every year, these challenges seem to be only growing more and more. We only have to look at the recent disasters; it’s quite terrifying for the people who are living in these landscapes.

For several reasons, it’s crucial that we recognize that our situation is changing and that it is very fragile, and we have to be alert to this changing situation. So much has already changed, and within this framework we have to think of how we are going to adapt to our new circumstances, whether it is living in the city, establishing a relationship with urban life, learning to operate in a language that is not your mother tongue, learning technology, issues of sustainability, and so on.

In the midst of this vast change from our previous ancestral way of life, how are we going to hold ourselves as people with a distinct way of living, language, and culture? Moreover, how are we going to maintain the values that have been passed down to us from our ancestors? How willing are we to work for our collective welfare to protect our cultural and food heritage in this sea of change? Because without addressing these questions or without internalizing them, we cannot have real progress.
Written by Sanjib Chaudhary

b6a152aa5fb65c1a: The state welcome accorded to French president Emmanuel Macron at Dataran Merdeka on Nov 17 reflected Malaysia’s growing strategic importance to France, a European country that is also an Indo-Pacific power.

France is not merely an external observer of the Indo-Pacific. Through its overseas territories, maritime interests, military presence and extensive exclusive economic zones, France has a permanent stake in the region. Malaysia, meanwhile, occupies one of Asia’s most consequential geographical positions.
It sits between the Straits of Malacca and the South China Sea, two maritime spaces indispensable to international commerce, energy security and regional stability.
The convergence of French strategic interests and Malaysia’s geographical significance creates opportunities for both countries to deepen their partnership.
France is an Indo-Pacific power

France possesses overseas territories in the Indian and Pacific Oceans, including Réunion, French Polynesia and New Caledonia. These territories give France a permanent population, maritime jurisdiction and security responsibilities across the Indo-Pacific.

Unlike European countries whose regional engagement depends primarily on diplomacy or commercial investment, France maintains a continuous physical presence. Its naval forces, surveillance capabilities and defence partnerships enable Paris to contribute to maritime security across vast distances.
Yet the Indo-Pacific cannot be secured through military deployments alone. The region requires diplomacy, economic connectivity, institutional cooperation and respect for international law.
This is where Malaysia becomes important.
Malaysia’s strategic geography

The Straits of Malacca is among the world’s most important maritime arteries. It connects the Indian Ocean to the South China Sea and the wider Pacific, facilitating trade between Europe, the Middle East, South Asia and East Asia.
Any serious disruption here would affect shipping costs, energy supplies and global supply chains. Malaysia shares responsibility for the security of this passage with Indonesia and Singapore.

Malaysia is both a maritime trading nation and a claimant state in the South China Sea. Its economic interests depend on freedom of navigation, uninterrupted commercial activity and the peaceful management of maritime disputes.

France therefore has compelling reasons to strengthen relations with Putrajaya. Malaysia offers Paris a diplomatic interlocutor linking the Indian and Pacific Oceans, while France gives Putrajaya another avenue for cooperation without excessive dependence on Washington or Beijing.
Beyond great-power rivalry
Competition between the US and China increasingly shapes the Indo-Pacific. Reducing the region to a binary confrontation, however, would be shortsighted.

France has traditionally emphasised strategic autonomy, even while remaining a member of Nato and a close US ally. Malaysia similarly values strategic independence and constructive relations with competing powers.
Both countries should recognise that smaller and medium-sized powers cannot be expected to surrender their national interests to the preferences of larger states.

Asean must remain central to regional diplomacy. France can support Asean-led institutions, including the East Asia Summit and Asean Regional Forum, while respecting the sovereignty of Southeast Asian countries.
The objective should not be to militarise the Indo-Pacific, but to strengthen a rules-based regional order through dialogue, confidence-building measures and practical cooperation.
Malaysia as a Europe-Asean bridge

This is where Malaysia can assume a more consequential diplomatic role. Its value to France should not be measured only by geography or bilateral trade. Malaysia can also serve as a bridge between European strategic interests and Asean's regional priorities.

Malaysia’s long-standing participation in Asean gives it an understanding of the region’s diplomatic sensitivities and diversity. Since Southeast Asian countries do not always share identical views on major-power competition or maritime disputes, European engagement must be based on consultation and respect for Asean centrality.

France can use its relationship with Malaysia to deepen its engagement with Southeast Asia. Putrajaya can help explain Asean's preference for inclusive dialogue and practical cooperation, while conveying European perspectives to regional partners.
This does not mean Malaysia should speak on behalf of every Asean member. Rather, it can help create channels through which European and Southeast Asian policymakers better understand one another.

The opportunity extends beyond France. As an EU member, France can contribute to stronger Asean-EU relations in maritime cooperation, digital governance, clean energy, education and resilient supply chains. These are areas of shared interest, but cooperation must be shaped around local needs and mutually agreed priorities.

Malaysia’s engagement with the EU provides a foundation. Stronger ties with France can connect governments, universities and businesses, turning diplomatic goodwill into sustained exchanges and practical projects.
A partnership across two strategic seas

Acting as a diplomatic bridge requires Malaysia to preserve its strategic autonomy, maintain constructive relations with major powers and remain committed to Asean-led processes. Its credibility rests on showing that cooperation need not force Southeast Asian countries into rival camps.

For France, this means engaging Malaysia as a partner with its own agency, not simply as a gateway for French influence. For Malaysia, it means widening its diplomatic and economic options while reinforcing Asean voice.

Ultimately, the significance of Macron’s visit should not be measured solely by the agreements announced. Its longer-term importance lies in whether Malaysia and France can build a partnership connecting two strategically important regions.

At the crossroads of the Straits of Malacca and the South China Sea, Malaysia can do more than safeguard maritime interests: it can help bring Europe and Asean closer through dialogue and practical cooperation.
