9aad3d1429562dda: Pakatan Harapan can blame racial politics, a polarised electorate, and the growing strength of its political rivals all it wants, but after another bruising defeat in Melaka, perhaps it's time the coalition look in the mirror.
Saturday's results saw Barisan Nasional win 21 seats, and its ally, Perikatan Nasional, three. PH's share was reduced to just four, one fewer than it secured in the 2021 polls.
It was another electoral setback following its poor showing in Johor and Negeri Sembilan.

Yet, if past experience is anything to go by, the coalition's post-mortem could once again revolve around familiar explanations: racial politics, the Malay vote, and its inability to penetrate the rural constituencies.
There is no denying that race and religion influence voters here, but these factors cannot forever serve as convenient explanations for PH's electoral shortcomings.
At what point does the coalition stop asking why voters are supposedly influenced by racial politics and start asking why those same voters are no longer convinced that PH deserves their support?
A coalition that has forgotten its promises
One of PH's biggest problems is its reluctance to confront the gap between what it promised before entering government and what it has delivered.
The coalition came to power in 2018 promising institutional reforms, greater accountability, transparency, and a cleaner political culture. But eight years later, how much of that enthusiasm remains?
PH cannot expect support simply because it once represented an alternative to BN.
It has been in government since November 2022, with Anwar Ibrahim as prime minister and its components holding important ministerial positions. It has had the opportunity to deliver on its promises.
Instead, voters are often given explanations about why reforms cannot be implemented or why political compromises are necessary.

Where are the apologies for promises that have been abandoned or watered down? Where is the sustained effort to reconnect with communities that feel neglected, not just when elections approach but throughout the term?
Perhaps the biggest contradiction is how PH has moved away from the principles it once championed.

The coalition previously fought for fairer parliamentary allocations, arguing that public funds should not be used as a political weapon against opposition MPs. Now, it withdraws the allocations for errant MPs.

Whatever the political justification, the irony is difficult to ignore. A coalition that once criticised the previous government for practising political discrimination now finds itself defending similar questions about the distribution of public resources.
Voters did not support PH merely to see a change in who exercises political power. They wanted a change in how that power was exercised.
The influencer experiment is backfiring
Another questionable aspect of PH's political strategy is its reliance on social media influencers and content creators.

There's nothing wrong with embracing digital campaigning, particularly to reach the younger voters. But there's a difference between using social media effectively and assuming trendy videos, scripted skits and supposedly relatable content will translate into political support.
During GE15, PH's campaign focused heavily on policy discussions, institutional reform, and fighting corruption. Today, some of its social media campaigning appears to have lost that seriousness.
PH has increasingly been associated with content that feels forced, cringey and disconnected from the supporters it's trying to engage. Even some PH supporters have criticised these efforts online.

Politicians aren't entertainers. A young voter struggling with stagnant wages, rising living costs and housing affordability is unlikely to be persuaded simply because a politician can perform a trending dance or deliver a rehearsed punchline.
PH appears to be mistaking social media engagement for genuine political engagement.
Parliament is not a ‘mamak' stall
The conduct of some PH MPs has also become increasingly difficult to defend.

Parliament should be where MPs debate policies, scrutinise legislation and raise the concerns of their constituents. While the opposition has MPs who rely on provocative rhetoric and attempts to bait government representatives, PH MPs should know better than to fall into the same trap.

The behaviour of certain representatives, including RSN Rayer (Jelutong) and Sany Hamzan (Hulu Langat), raises questions about whether they understand the difference between robust parliamentary debate and simply creating a commotion.
There's nothing wrong with being vocal or combative, but there must be substance behind the noise.

Voters want to hear what their MPs are doing about public transport, unemployment, housing and healthcare. They don't elect representatives to turn parliamentary proceedings into something resembling a heated argument at a mamak stall.
Candidate selection isn't a social media experiment
The Melaka election also exposed weaknesses in PH's candidate selection.

Giving younger candidates an opportunity is commendable, but youth alone should never be the qualification for public office. Candidates must be properly vetted and demonstrate an understanding of the communities they intend to represent.

One candidate who attracted attention for the wrong reasons was Mukhlisul Mubin Julasapiyah (Kuala Linggi), better known as Mukhlis Mubin. His campaign leaned heavily into a Gen Z identity, complete with the tagline, "This is how Gen Z works".
A campaign video attracted mixed reactions after he claimed to have secured a waiver of a penalty exceeding RM70,000 imposed on the Melaka Barat Area Fishermen's Association within a day.
Mukhlis said he approached Anwar's political secretary, who brought the matter to Anwar in his capacity as finance minister, who subsequently approved the waiver.
While helping an association representing 278 fishermen was commendable, the episode raised questions about the use of political connections to secure preferential treatment.
Critics questioned whether this was cronyism rather than the institutional reforms PH had promised.
There were also questions about his candidacy, given that his father had contested Kuala Linggi five times without winning.

PH must ask whether it selected candidates based on their ability to win public confidence or simply because they fitted a particular campaign narrative. An assemblyman needs considerably more than attractive online content to represent an entire constituency.
The electorate doesn't owe PH another chance
Another longstanding weakness is PH's grassroots machinery. The coalition cannot expect to build relationships through occasional visits and staged community engagements.
BN and PAS spent decades building networks through local leaders, party branches and community organisations. That machinery does not suddenly appear two weeks before polling day.

PH must understand that political loyalty is built through consistency, not campaign-season appearances. Perhaps the most uncomfortable truth the coalition needs to accept is that voters don't owe it their loyalty.
Those who supported PH in 2018 did so because they believed it could deliver a better Malaysia. They weren't signing a lifetime commitment to a party.
Some voters may not have rejected its reform agenda. They may simply have become disillusioned with the people entrusted to implement it.

Melaka should be more than another electoral setback followed by post-mortem meetings and familiar explanations. PH needs to take a hard look at its leadership, candidates, grassroots machinery, parliamentary conduct and, most importantly, its record in government.

Race and religion will remain part of Malaysian politics. But blaming racial politics every time voters turn away is not political analysis. It is an admission that the coalition has run out of answers.
PH once asked Malaysians to believe that a different kind of politics was possible. Now it must prove that that vision still deserves belief.
The question is no longer why voters are abandoning PH but why PH keeps giving them reasons to do so.
The writer is a journalist at FMT’s English Desk.

bccee91cf8115d86: Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company's vision for its new "frontier ecosystem," announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as "the new OS for work."

The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent's work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.
92da6fb1944da7be: I watched the Bollywood film Ramayana last week and it was well worth the money. I went for a late morning show to avoid the crowd but was surprised to find only six families and a couple.
What was even more surprising—and pleasantly so—was the racial mixture of this small audience: three Indian families, a Chinese family, two Malay families, and an older Malay couple.

Why not? I thought. After all, the Ramayana didn’t just visit the Malay world; for centuries, it lived here. It was woven into the fabric of village life, shaped the language of court chronicles, and danced across white screens of buffalo skin in flickering torchlight.
Then again, I noted that only a very small number of Malays had ventured to watch the movie which had received rave reviews.

That made me think more deeply and I realised that the Ramayana in Malaysia today is a ghost story of culture—how an epic of foreign origin was lovingly adopted by the Malays, only to be quietly pushed to the margins by modern politics and shifting religious boundaries.
How did an epic composed in ancient India find its way into the hearts of Malay villagers and sultans?

Its journey happened in two distinct waves. Long before written books were common, the first wave arrived during the first millennium CE through maritime trade. Traders and travellers brought Indian culture, statecraft, and stories to early coastal trading centres such as Kedah Tua, Gangga Negara and Langkasuka, embedding foundational ideas into local life.

Centuries later came the second wave: the vernacular transformation. As scholar Alexander Zieseniss pointed out in his 1963 study, what reached the Malay world wasn't the classical Sanskrit text, but popular, post-epic oral versions carried by word of mouth from India.

You can still hear that journey in the names preserved in early Malay adaptations: Baradan, Wibisana, Maharaja Rawana, and Kumbakarna point directly to Tamil roots, proving the tales travelled through South Indian oral channels before anyone here ever wrote them down.

The result was the Hikayat Seri Rama, written in Jawi script. In a wonderful twist of global history, the oldest surviving illuminated manuscript of this text—dating back to around 1600 from the Aceh Sultanate—was brought to England by a trading sea-captain and eventually found its way to Archbishop William Laud, who donated it to Oxford’s Bodleian Library between 1635 and 1641.

While British colonial scholars like Richard Winstedt once framed this through the lens of Muslim courts simply "tolerating" old Hindu tales, modern historians see it as dynamic syncretisation. Local scribes and courts didn't feel conflicted; they indigenised the story, folding its heroes and moral dilemmas right into the Malay worldview.
In traditional literature, the Ramayana – which scholar C Hooykaas said “belongs to all ages and all creeds”- was a vital structural pillar.
Literary historians agree that these epics provided the foundational narrative DNA for classic court chronicles like the Sejarah Melayu and the Hikayat Hang Tuah.

Linguistically, the epic helped carry valuable Sanskrit vocabulary into the Malay language. While laksamana (traditionally derived from Rama’s loyal brother Lakshmana and historically used for admirals) is the most famous surviving direct borrowing, a whole vocabulary of statecraft, ethics, and storytelling entered everyday speech through this deep cultural exchange.
If court literature was where the epic found its intellect, the agrarian villages of northeastern Malaya were where it found its heartbeat.

For generations, wayang kulit Kelantan (traditional shadow puppetry) was not a museum piece or high art; it was community life. Imagine an all-night village performance under the stars. A single master dalang (puppet master) would sit behind a backlit cloth, single-handedly voicing dozens of characters while blending the grand plots of the Ramayana with local folklore, village humour, and Thai-Kelantanese aesthetics.

As traditional arts expert Ghulam-Sarwar Yousof noted, these epics provided the bulk of the raw material for the region's traditional theatre. In the villages of Kelantan, the Ramayana wasn't a foreign import. It was “our story”, performed collectively, without any modern anxieties about theological purity.

The fading of this vibrant tradition wasn't a natural accident of time. Shifting religious definitions in the latter half of the 20th century, especially from the 1980s, began to recast traditional folk arts through a narrower ideological lens.
The numbers tell a stark story. In 1969, Kelantan boasted around 300 active dalang. By the 1999 census, that number had plummeted to just 11 troupes.

While informal pressures accumulated soon after the Islamist party PAS came to power in Kelantan in 1990, the heavy blow landed legally with the 1998 Entertainment Enactment, which officially banned wayang kulit performances for containing "un-Islamic" elements - such as animist healing invocations and Hindu mythological roots.

Though the state government formally lifted the ban in 2019, it came with heavy strings attached: performances were only permitted under strict Shariah-compliant conditions, creating ongoing bureaucratic hurdles for traditional masters.

Today, only a tiny handful of senior dalang remain active in Kota Bharu, while Malaysia's national bid for UNESCO intangible cultural heritage status for the Kelantanese shadow play sits patiently pending.
Today too, active daily engagement with the Ramayana among the majority Malay population is practically zero. The living village tradition has faded under decades of regulatory constraints.
Yet the story hasn’t entirely vanished; it lingers in the background of modern life through regional identity, digital preservation, and occasional pop-culture references.

This is what I saw in the theatre that day. The Malays in the audience simply watched the spectacle as large-format entertainment—nothing more, nothing less, yet the myth's invisible threads ran right through the room. For I overheard the gentleman next to me telling his wife that Jatayu would come to the abducted Sita’s aid even before Jatayu’s appearance on screen.

Which reassured me that although it is not vibrantly alive in the way it once was, the Ramayana in Malaysia is not completely dead. It stands as a quiet, beautiful ghost story of culture—a reminder of a pluralistic past that still echoes softly in the dark of a cinema.

b96ca28a538fdb15: Kata beberapa penganalisis politik dan penyelidik termasuk daripada Ilham Centre, Barisan Nasional (BN) khususnya Umno, tetap boleh menang PRN Melaka tempoh hari walaupun bertanding solo. Begitu jugalah keadaannya di Johor dan Negeri Sembilan sebelum ini, kata mereka.
Ya, saya tahu ini membuat pemimpin, ahli dan penyokong PN terutama PAS marah. Apa lagi ketika pemimpin BN dan PN cukup yakin gandingan mereka boleh membawa kejayaan merampas Putrajaya.

Meskipun berkata apa yang mereka kata yang disebut tadi, penganalisis dan penyelidik juga berkata kerjasama BN-PN memang beri impak kemenangan besar kepada kedua-dua parti atau lebih tepat gabungan politik berkenaan. Benar ini sudah dilihat.

Bagaimanapun, menurut salah seorang daripada penganalisis itu (ini memang bikin panas PAS, sama ada pemimpin, ahli mahupun penyokong), PAS-PN tidak akan menang sebarang kerusi jika bergerak solo pada PRN Melaka.
Menurut beliau, gelombang hijau semakin pudar, majoriti pengundi Umno yang mengundi PN pada PRN 2021 dan PRU 2022 kembali mengundi BN pada PRN kali ini.
“Itu dalam konteks Melaka. Sokongan Melayu, banyak pengundi teras adalah BN, bukan PAS. PRN dan PRU lalu banyak undi protes Umno-BN pergi ke PN-PAS. Sekarang kembali ke pangkuan BN," katanya.

Memang ada benar pandangan beliau. Namun pada PRN Melaka yang baru berlalu, PAS hanya bertanding dua kerusi. Maka tidak banyak 'peluang' untuk pengundi teras Umno beri 'sumbangan' kepada parti itu. Atau membuktikan semangat 'kesetiakawanan'.
Namun PAS menang jua di dua-dua kerusi. Wawasan, rakan PAS dalam PN juga menang, tapi satu kerusi sahajalah. Satu lagi komponen – Gerakan – seperti dijangka, tak menang apa-apa.

Apa pun mesti diakui, Melaka dan Johor memang kubu BN. Jadi betullah apa yang dikata penganalisis bahawa BN/Umno boleh menang on its own di kedua-dua negeri itu. I’m not sure about Negeri Sembilan. Tetapi jika tidak mahu melabel Negeri Sembilan 'kubu' BN, perlu diakui ia (baca: Umno) kuat di negeri itu.
Dalam konteks kerjasama BN-PN, persoalan yang sering timbul untuk sekian lama adalah siapa tolong siapa lebih. Kerjasama lebih menguntungkan Umno-BN atau PAS-PN?
Kerap ditanya juga ialah soal transferability undi, yakni mana lebih banyak? Undi asal Umno pergi ke PAS atau undi asal PAS pergi ke Umno?

Tentu kita ingat Presiden PAS Hadi Awang beberapa kali menyeru ahli dan penyokong partinya mengundi BN di kawasan PAS tidak bertanding. Seruan beliau dibuat terbuka dengan lantang. Malah beliau turut meminta ahli dan penyokong PAS mengundi MCA dan MIC kerana 'mereka BN'.
Pernahkah pemimpin tertinggi Umno buat saranan ala Hadi? Iaitu meminta ahli dan penyokongnya undi PAS pada ketika Umno-BN tidak letak calon.
Setahu saya tidak. Adakah saya terlepas pandang dan terlepas dengar? Wallahua'lam.
Tetapi pada PRN Johor, Negeri Sembilan dan Melaka, bilangan calon Umno-BN melebihi calon PAS-PN. Di Johor, PAS-PN bertanding di 11 kerusi sahaja daripada jumlah 56 DUN.
Di Negeri Sembilan, PAS-PN tanding lima kerusi out of 36 seats in the state assembly. Manakala di Melaka, ada 28 kerusi DUN, PAS-PN tanding lima kerusi.

Saya beberapa kali menyatakan kerjasama Umno-BN dengan PAS-PN berjaya terjalin kerana PAS yang banyak mengalah. Parti itu tidak buat tuntutan (setakat ini), rela beri laluan kepada Umno-BN, tunduk akur meskipun dapat pittance. Needless to say, ahli parti tidak suka akan arrangement sebegitu. Ini diakui Hadi. Tetapi diteruskan juga 'demi Islam memerintah'.
Namun, saya sering juga tanya sampai bila PAS akan mengalah? Pada hemat saya, akan tiba masa PAS akan buat demand when the right time comes. By that I meant, pilihan PRU mendatang.
Bercakap mengenai PRU akan datang, lebih tepat PRU16, saya amat tertarik dengan kenyataan pengerusi BN yang juga Presiden Umno Zahid Hamidi yang disiar Malaysiakini tiga hari lalu.

Zahid dilaporkan berkata, BN belum merancang membentuk kerjasama atau persefahaman politik dengan PN bagi menghadapi PRU16. Ini bukanlah memeranjatkan kerana mungkin terlalu awal untuk bercakap mengenai PRU at this time.

Namun, hanya beberapa hari sebelum itu Zahid berkata, kemenangan di Melaka, yakni yang ketiga berturut turut selepas Johor dan Negeri Sembilan, ialah kesinambungan gelombang biru dan langkah penting menuju ke Putrajaya. Gelombang biru kita tahu terjadi hasil kerjasama BN-PN. Lalu saya ulang tanya – siapa lebih banyak tolong siapa?

Kata beliau, apa yang dilalui khususnya untuk PRN Negeri Sembilan dan Melaka adalah apa yang beliau namakan 'tafahum siyasi' atau kesefahaman politik. “Kita belum pernah merancang untuk ke arah yang lebih jauh." Pulak dah. Belum pernah? Seriously?
Tetapi Zahid mengakui, jika tiba masanya dan keadaan memerlukan 'kita akan duduk bersama sama'. Ini typical political talk oleh sang politikus.

Namun, ia boleh mencetuskan pelbagai interpretasi dan spekulasi. Antaranya, adakah BN mahu guna kemenangan tiga PRN berturut-turut sebagai bargaining chip dalam membuat beberapa tuntutan apabila berunding dengan Pakatan Harapan? Ketika PH berada at its lowest ebb?
Bagaimana agaknya reaksi PAS terhadap kenyataan Zahid? Kepimpinan tertingginya mempunyai high hopes of bringing the BN-PN cooperation to the next level.
Entah entah Zahid pun dapat 'intel' Umno-BN 'sebenarnya' boleh menang di Johor, Negeri Sembilan dan Melaka kalaupun tanding solo. Yakni, without PAS-PN. Lantas beliau dah mula naik syok kot?
Tetapi, ini hanya di tiga negeri di mana BN memang kuat. Di Melaka umpamanya semasa PRN 2021 BN juga menang 21 kerusi. Jadi, 21 kerusi yang BN menang pada PRN tahun ini bererti status quo.
Hakikatnya, BN-Umno tidak kuat atau belum cukup kuat. Memang kalau boleh ia mahu tanding solo. Tetapi BN-Umno masih perlukan PN-PAS. Begitu juga PN-PAS yang perlukan BN-Umno.
Namun, itu pun belum boleh guarantee mereka menang kerana ada 1,001 masalah. Ini kita cerita lain kali.

f38228c9ef565932: MIT students are going to office hours less often. They’re spending less time working through problem sets, and with one another. Those were among the findings of MIT’s recent report on artificial intelligence and education, and they are one reason a growing number of MIT faculty are concerned about how generative AI is both changing how people work and affecting how they think, learn, and relate to one another. For the MIT Human Insight Collaborative (MITHIC), those questions have become a central focus, and MITHIC is working with collaborators across the Institute, including the Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing (SERC), to help MIT address them. Launched in 2024 as a strategic initiative, MITHIC brings together scholars, artists, educators, and researchers to explore the human dimensions of the defining challenges of our time. Since its launch, MITHIC has supported 67 projects across 31 MIT units, offering a total of $5.5 million in funding. Roughly a third of those projects are focused on AI, society, and humanity — a topic that MITHIC faculty co-lead Heather Paxson says has become an increasingly important part of the initiative. “When we refer to AI and society, we’re not only speaking about individual ethical decision-making or how to retrain workers. We’re looking at how AI is reshaping sociality, how we relate to one another,” says Paxson, a professor of anthropology and the associate dean of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS).  Eroding “creative friction”  Building upon this focus, an AI and Society Forum took place on campus earlier this year. Co-organized by MITHIC, SHASS, SERC, and the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium (MGAIC), the event featured presentations and panels concentrating on jobs, democracy, and AI.  On campus, the report on AI and education warned that AI is eroding the “creative friction” that has long defined an MIT education: students debating ideas and challenging one another, their professors, and their teaching assistants, in class and out of it. MITHIC faculty co-lead Seth Mnookin, a science writing professor and head of Comparative Media Studies Program/Writing (CMS/W), said, “The report wasn’t saying that AI is here and we all need to adapt. It was saying that we need to be asking more fundamental questions.”   “When the United States entered World War II in 1941, the Institute’s newly minted scientists and engineers helped shape that era through science and technology,” Mnookin said. “We’re at a similarly consequential moment with AI. The difference is that this time, the questions that matter most can’t be answered by technologists alone. That’s where the humanities, arts, and social sciences come in.” Crossing disciplines in the pursuit of answers MITHIC is supporting a range of interdisciplinary projects through its SHASS+ Connectivity Fund, in which a SHASS scholar partners with a researcher in another part of MIT.  In the context of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, political science professors Adam Berinsky and Charles Stewart III and MIT Sloan School of Management Assistant Professor Chara Podimata are studying how large language models (LLMs) have become intermediaries of democratic knowledge.  The ongoing project, which has demonstrated how voters in Alaska’s midterms who conducted their pre-election research using Anthropic’s AI model, Claude, may have received incomplete information about candidates and their views, was recently featured in The New York Times.  “AI is becoming part of the way people encounter and make sense of political information, and yet we know relatively little about what that information environment actually looks like, how it differs for different user demographics, political identities, and geographies,” Podimata told the Times. In another project, CMS/W Professor Eric Klopfer and brain and cognitive sciences Professor Pawan Sinha are co-leading research that’s measuring AI’s near- and long-term effects on cognition. Meeting at the intersection of AI, education, and neuroscience, the professors are examining whether generative AI is increasing the human brain’s consumption of information but offloading cognitive function, or supporting an increase in cognitive function when used as part of the creative process. They recently gathered experts on the topic for an event on the MIT campus, “AI and the Brain.” In the field of arts and technology, Anna Huang, a professor of music technology holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Joe Paradiso, a professor at the MIT Media Lab, are examining how incorporating AI impacts the creative process and live performance experience. Their project, “Live Musician-AI Improvisation, Tuning the Social Aesthetics in Human-AI Partnerships” explores the question: what happens when human composers and contemporary machine learning systems improvise to make music together?  As part of their project, a collective of MIT musicians, ethnomusicologists, and engineers meets for regular sessions to experiment with improvisation frameworks like stopping to discuss how technology impacts authorship and musical direction, ensemble dynamics, and other cornerstones of improvisation. Faculty will ultimately incorporate their takeaways into a future course or practicum on AI-improvisation. Teaching and scholarship in an AI era SHASS faculty and academic staff are also leading new MITHIC initiatives to help broaden instruction and community dialogue about the intersection of AI and society.  Graham Jones, professor of anthropology, and Arvind Satyanarayan, associate professor of computer science, used MITHIC’s SHASS+ Connectivity funding to help launch a course, 6.S061/21A.S02 (Humane User Experience Design), in which students examine how AI systems are designed and grapple with the consequences of AI agents entering into socio-cultural relationships with people through their ability to mimic human thought and speech. “The crux of our collaboration is the term 'humane.' It’s a bit of a double-entendre, meaning both human-serving or benevolent, and humanlike,” Jones said at the inaugural MITHIC Annual Event. “What’s interesting is that our students are discovering that there’s a fundamental tension between building a system that’s good for people and one that seems human, because real people can develop dangerous dependencies.” Another project, “Rebuilding Computing and Society at MIT,” is supported by MITHIC’s Education Impact Fund (EIF). Led by Dwai Banerjee, associate professor of science, technology, and society, the initiative revitalized the Computing and Society concentration launched in 2019. The HASS concentration had gone dormant, listing classes no longer being offered and with minimal student interest. The concentration now features current classes across 11 SHASS units in which students can explore computing through different humanistic and social science angles. Banerjee, who serves as the concentration’s advisor, is also working with lecturer and research affiliate Mariel Garcia-Montes PhD ’26 to find ways to connect the concentration instructors and campus initiatives on computing and society. MIT senior Daniel Gonzalez is also part of the project, developing a research and outreach program that centers undergraduate voices in computing and society efforts across the Institute. Another MITHIC project funded by the EIF, “Review of Generative AI Assistive and Resistant Communication Assignments and Supporting Workshops,” is led by Michael Trice, a lecturer in MIT’s Writing, Rhetoric, and Professional Communication (WRAP) program. The project is responding to a consistent SHASS faculty request for additional training and skills needed “to fully address generative AI concerns in their classes.”  Trice is creating a bank of faculty resources and facilitating workshops and visiting lectures on generative AI and writing. These include a talk given earlier this fall by John Gallagher from the University of Illinois, who presented findings from a large-scale survey on AI-usage and writing conducted with undergraduates at his institution in 2026. Meeting the moment MIT leaders agree that MITHIC, now in its third year, is playing a central role in the Institute meeting the moment, as AI presents both extraordinary potential and disturbing risks.  “There has never been a more important time for constructive collaboration between science and technology and the human-centered disciplines,” MIT President Sally Kornbluth recently said. “Through MITHIC, MIT is giving faculty the support to reach out across disciplines and pursue their dreams.” Agustín Rayo, dean of SHASS and co-chair of MITHIC, agrees. “MIT is uniquely placed to help us understand this extraordinary moment and to generate the values, tools, and policies that we will need to shape AI so that it becomes a force for good,” he said. “It is essential that we deploy AI technology in a way that elevates human existence, rather than diminishing it.” At the recent SHASS 75th Anniversary Symposium, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan said given the rapid development of AI, an understanding of the ethical implications and societal impact of implementing new technologies is especially urgent. “SHASS provides an essential perspective on questions concerning how technology can be developed thoughtfully and deployed responsibly, with the aim of improving human well-being,” said Chandrakasan, who also serves as MITHIC co-chair. Looking ahead, MITHIC and SERC are developing a series of events that pair humanists or social scientists with colleagues in a single field, starting with mathematics, to examine what AI is changing about how that field produces knowledge and trains its next generation. “The question isn’t whether AI will change these fields,” Mnookin said. “It’s whether we understand what’s at stake before it does.”

01d6eb729a095e9d: Huang is hardly the first powerful person to lower their defenses. Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesThe end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony. The chief executive of a company whose growth has been propelled by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature. Huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he co-founded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The company says no secrets were leaked. In a world increasingly focused on protecting private information against high-tech hacking schemes, Huang’s downfall is a reminder that, as the infamous hacker Kevin Mitnick observed, the “human factor is truly security’s weakest link.” Huang is hardly the first person in a powerful position to lower their defenses. In 2023, Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation. In 2011, former CIA Director David Petraeus gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information. These cases raise an important question: Why would someone with an entire security apparatus at their disposal let their guard down in an ordinary conversation or an intimate moment? Part of the answer comes down to the ways in which we are wired to react to other human beings. As a social psychologist who studies how people respond to requests, I’ve seen how a human voice, a simple touch or the mere physical presence of another person can be persuasive. Social cues that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy can make people feel safer, more trusting – and more willing to hand over money, comply with requests, divulge information or take risks. The comfort of a human voice Mitnick has been called “the most notorious hacker of all time.” Until his arrest in 1995, he spent years gaining access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola. He pulled off his espionage not by writing sophisticated code-breaking software but by having conversations with his targets. He would call people up and talk them into handing over their passwords by claiming to be the new IT guy or someone’s boss’s colleague. The people he spoke to overwhelmingly believed him. In other words, Mitnick recognized the power of the human voice. Studies show that hearing a person’s voice, as compared to reading their written thoughts, makes that person seem more capable and relatable. Interactions via phone, video chat and voice chat also create stronger social bonds than the same kinds of interactions via text or email. Perhaps for these reasons, people are more effective at persuading others to do things for them over the phone compared to when they make the same requests by text. In a study I conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad, participants asked other people for favors through randomly assigned communication channels. They received about twice as many “yes” responses over the phone as they did by email. When it comes to obtaining company secrets or circumventing export laws, a human voice may be all you need. And that isn’t the only edge people have. The Midas touch Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects on tipping behavior, acquiescence and risk-taking. In a famous 1984 study, a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips. In another classic psychology study, female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone. When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change. The researchers theorized that these light touches created a sense of familiarity. That familiarity, in turn, made people more willing to open their wallets. Other research suggests that light touch can also make people feel safer and more willing to take risks. In a 2010 study, participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder. A reassuring touch can make people more generous and more willing to take risks. abezikus/iStock via Getty Images The power of face-to-face Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment, illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about. In the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant. The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks. Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting. In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone. In this version, only 22.5% went that far. Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings, my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face. In one study, participants who made requests in person were 34 times more likely to get a yes than those who made requests by email. In another study, in-person requests were significantly more effective than requests made over the phone or video call. Cyberattacks and phishing emails pose real threats to security. But sometimes the biggest threats come from the people in the room with you. While we don’t know exactly what transpired between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, her proximity to the Nvidia CEO illustrates a vulnerability that even the best cybersecurity measures can struggle to guard against. 1d3650fe9301a9a2: Got home last night at midnight cause the Amtrak from Philly was a disaster (I’ll ignore the coincidences for now)1. So the longer discussion on Biases, Filter Bubbles ,and Investing Errors will have to wait.

Right on cue, this beauty popped up. The problem is less about the chart itself than it is about the accompanying headline: These Charts Show How More People Are Pulling Cash Out of Their Homes. The Journal noted that “Home equity lines of credit are becoming popular again as people try to avoid giving up their low-rate primary mortgages.”

I beg to differ. That chart above was what the Journal began the piece with. To my eye, it looks like Home Equity has ~tracked the underlying value of mortgage debt, which we know tracks the value of residential real estate.
If Equity is ~72% of total value now, that is where it was at the 2022 peak ($32T of $44T). It was 63% in 2019, 46% at the 2012 trough, and about 60% in 2000 and 2006-07.

Mortgage debt is up from roughly $12T to $14T since 2022, about 14%, and total housing value rose about the same 14%. So debt is growing in line with values, and the loan-to-value ratio is flat at around 28%.
How is that evidence of owners extracting more equity? Yes, more on an ABSOLUTE basis, but that’s not newsworthy; it’s GDP growth and inflation.
This reminds me of the NYSE Margin panic we see from time to time. Contrary to some innumerate claims, record rising NYSE margin was nothing to worry about; this was back in 2015.

Show me that the percentage of home equity is increasing faster than the underlying value of homes — and you have something. But rising more or less in line with Home values just means the entire RRE pie is getting bigger — mortgages AND home equity? Nothing to see there.
One question that came up in Philly about How Not to Invest involved bad charts. My answer was: “If a picture is worth a 1000 words, a Chart Crime equals 1000 lies...”

a3cb9e0745e497c9: In recent days, Iran-backed Houthi forces have gained greater control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital hub of trade, travel and migration between the Middle East and Africa. The partial closing of the Strait of Hormuz as part of the war in Iran – and escalating conflicts in Yemen, Ethiopia and Eritrea – had already brought this narrow waterway into new global prominence. Control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains critical to military operations and commodity markets throughout the region. However, the Bab el-Mandeb’s strategic geopolitical and commercial shipping importance has largely overshadowed its role as a critical humanitarian corridor. Bab el-Mandeb means “gate of lamentation” or, more poetically, “gate of tears” in Arabic. It remains one of the most dangerous migration passages in the world. Last year, more than 900 people died or went missing trying to cross. In October 2026, a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti carrying nearly 300 people, many of whom were escaping violence and persecution. Meanwhile, millions of people in Yemen and throughout the Horn of Africa face destitution or death without access to lifesaving deliveries of humanitarian relief supplies shipped through the strait. Our years of research and forthcoming book “Refugees Without Refuge” demonstrate how the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is key to the lives of millions of people throughout the region seeking safety, opportunity and humanitarian assistance. Protecting the safe movement of people and goods through the strait is key to averting future tragedies. A corridor for travel, trade and escape Located at the southern mouth of the Red Sea, between the arid coastlines of Eritrea, Djibouti and Yemen, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and Suez Canal. On a clear day along the wide beaches and mangrove forests on the coast of Djibouti, you can see the sandy hills on the shores of Yemen, only about 20 to 30 miles away. On starry nights, the scattered lights of coastal towns twinkle across the waters. For centuries, passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has been vital to global trade in salt, spices, coffee, livestock and other goods. Religious pilgrims, travelers, migrants and traders have long used the strait for relatively easy transport between continents. Today, people crossing the strait are also escaping poverty, war, political persecution, disasters and gender-based violence. Hot, tired, financially depleted and frequently sick or injured, refugees and migrants traverse the Bab el-Mandeb at all hours. Most negotiate passage across the strait on derelict boats with “delalas” – facilitators, brokers or smugglers – in the shadows of coast guard and police patrols and outside United Nations and governmental migration controls. The numbers of people crossing the strait are difficult to estimate. Between January and August 2026, the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration recorded 122,258 arrivals to Yemen from the Horn of Africa – even more than had crossed by that time in 2025. Most of these migrants were from Ethiopia, and most traveled without passports or visas. Since August, displacement and insecurity throughout the region has worsened, making accurate figures for the numbers of people migrating and the numbers of people dying trying to cross impossible to estimate. A lifeline for those escaping conflict Despite the dangers of this crossing, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains an economic lifeline for millions of people living in Ethiopia, Kenya, Somaliland, Somalia and elsewhere who rely on commercial goods imported from the Middle East and Asia. However, the Houthi forces in charge of increasing swaths of southwestern Yemen now control most critical ports and islands in the strait, increasing the risks and costs of transit and trade. The strait has either been closed or has become a bottleneck, allowing only limited shipping traffic since September 2026. Many cargo ships have been delayed or rerouted, causing businesses in fragile regional economies to pass higher transport and fuel costs on to their customers. The economic effects of costly and delayed shipping and trade through the strait has compounded the broader effects of increased violence and displacement throughout the region. In front of the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 26, 2026, Djibouti foreign minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar expressed “grave concern” about the sudden influx of Yemeni refugees putting a strain on underresourced coastal towns and refugee camps. The United Nations relief agency, UNHCR, is reporting an outbreak of cholera in the Markazi refugee camp, the primary home to thousands of Yemenis who have fled across the strait into northern Djibouti. Members of the Djiboutian coast guard inspect boats seized from ‘delalas’ attempting to transport migrants to Yemen on April 12, 2026. Luis Tato/AFP via Getty Images On top of that, the potential for a return to civil war in Ethiopia, and the potential involvement of Eritrea in regional conflicts, may increase population displacement and further disrupt economic markets on both sides of the strait. As each of these conflicts unfolds, additional pressure will likely be put on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. It provides the only feasible passage for many people seeking safety and opportunity abroad. A humanitarian corridor Keeping the Bab el-Mandeb open and safe is also vital for the delivery of humanitarian aid. Like challenges of commercial shipping, the maritime transit of relief supplies, including food and medicine, has been undermined by security risks, shipping delays and the rising costs of food and fuel. UNICEF’s latest situation report for Somalia, published in August 2026, estimates that nearly 5 million people there are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. At least another 5.5 million people in Ethiopia are also in need, due to the effects of conflict combined with below-average rainfall linked to El Niño. In Yemen, an estimated 321,000 people have been displaced since Aug. 1, 2026, and ongoing water scarcity combined with conflict has left 17 million people without access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene services. As casualties mount and cholera spreads, hospitals have struggled to obtain essential supplies. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait sits at the center of all of these crises. It remains a vital human and humanitarian corridor for millions of people needing refuge and relief. It is a lifeline as much as a geopolitical and economic linchpin. Ensuring the safe passage of people and supplies of humanitarian relief through these waters is necessary to save lives and protect precarious livelihoods throughout the region. 47a7c5b0482b14c4: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.

Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River. And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.

Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.
Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.

Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.

The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.

But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study. Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.
Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.

El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions.

Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.
bfe144881fd661a3: It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design. The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.

The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.

As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You'll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It's under Activity in the Gemini settings. You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.

82a0f3f376656399: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. ffe4b9c88a23c6ca: John Urschel PhD ’21, the Class of 1956 Career Development Assistant Professor in the MIT Department of Mathematics, is no stranger to building muscle: Before earning his PhD at MIT, Urschel strengthened his offensive muscles as a lineman for the Baltimore Ravens. He remains committed to helping his students exercise, but now his focus is on critical thinking skills. In the classroom, Urschel shares with his students his lifelong love for solving puzzles, while honing their abilities to be strong quantitative thinkers — skills he argues will be essential in an artificial intelligence-enabled world.  Urschel recently published two preprints on arXiv, one on the growth factor of random matrices, the other on worst-case behavior in Gaussian elimination, in which he used a combination of human insight and AI tools to solve problems that had stumped mathematicians for decades. That experience provided Urschel with new insights into the future of mathematics and higher education, and the enduring importance of the in-person, residential education offered on college campuses, where students can experience the importance of struggle, problem solving, and human connection. Urschel recently chatted with MIT News about education, AI, and mathematics; excerpts from the conversation follow.  Q: What is it about studying math that you hope to share with your students? A: When I was very little, I loved solving puzzles, whether that’s Sudoku puzzles or Martin Gardner math puzzles or crossword puzzles. I think there’s something really enjoyable about being faced with some problem that you don’t quite understand, trying to get your bearings, trying to make your way through it, and finally gleaning some sort of understanding from it. That’s a process that I’ve enjoyed for as long as I can remember, and that’s the thing that I’ve really enjoyed most about math. When it comes to teaching, first, I want to help our students train themselves and hone their ability to solve problems and their ability to be strong quantitative thinkers. The second part, which is more specific to whichever course I’m teaching, is to help them assimilate the big ideas or tools or techniques or themes that help them become better problem solvers in that specific discipline. If they’re taking a course on a specific subject, the idea is for me to try to convey important fundamentals so that they can use that learned expertise to become better problem solvers out in the world. Q: You recently used AI to assist in solving two proofs. Can you talk a bit about the experience? A: These are the first two papers where I’ve ever touched the machine, and it does feel different. It’s not unlike having a collaborator, but it’s a collaborator who has access to unlimited resources, seemingly, and does certain things much, much faster than I ever could.  In the same way that computers can do calculations much faster than any of us can, I think at this point it’s very clear that artificial intelligence systems can do certain types of mathematics much, much more efficiently than any of us can.  Q: What was it like using AI to solve math problems? Was it just as rewarding? A: For me, personally, I would say that the feeling that I talked about of problem solving, of thinking your way through a problem, I find that that’s most joyful for me when I do that by myself, without AI.  One thing that I think is really important is to have an independent sense of problem-solving ability, a sense of curiosity — this idea of building those mathematics muscles, which I think are important, even in the era of AI. Especially when you are talking with a machine, asking the machine for things, I think it’s very important to elevate the idea of understanding. If you’re talking to a machine, let’s say, and it gives you a proof of some mathematical fact, I think the true value in that proof comes from a human understanding and assimilating the way in which the machine combines certain mathematical ideas, and then internalizing that and communicating that knowledge to others. Understanding is the big thing that I stress to my students who use AI systems. And then for the students who do not use AI systems, I focus on building their problem-solving abilities, which is what we’ve done for centuries in mathematics.  I think in the age of modern AI machines, as long as there is a role for humans to think and try to solve problems, which I believe there is, then building these skills remains important. Q: The recent report from MIT’s Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning and Research Training stressed the importance of experiencing the necessary and productive struggle of learning, along with the collaborative aspect of learning. I’m curious what you think about the role of AI in math education going forward.  A: On one hand, the development of AI technologies should be viewed as a giant win for education, a giant win for leveling playing fields when you have technology that’s easily accessible, that gives you access to vast amounts of knowledge.  Neither of my parents are professors; I remember when I was a kid, I didn’t know what a mathematician was until I got to college. And the way I learned about advanced mathematical concepts in high school, but also when I got to college, was with a laptop, and with Google. I was able to Google some topic I want to learn about, and it was amazing that I could find papers written by some of the world’s leading experts, just freely available online at my fingertips to learn from. That was really important for me and so helpful for my education. But I think we’re at a point where modern technology is a bit of a double-edged sword. Because on one hand, with AI systems you can learn something faster than ever, and the resources I had when I was a kid would seem like small potatoes compared to the sorts of things you can do to help yourself learn nowadays.  But the issue is that this also can take away your ability to think and learn for yourself. I think it’s hard if you’re a high school student or you’re a college student. You have a lot going on, you’re tired, and thanks to AI, you can just finish your homework with the push of a button. You can write your 10-page essay with the push of a button. Also, you can get the false impression that you more or less understand what’s going on when you really don’t. I think that’s one of the big dangers when you don’t try to learn things for yourself.  People don’t like the word “struggle.” But when you don’t struggle with a certain material on your own, I think you can get the impression of learning without actually learning. Connecting with the material and really pushing yourself, that’s quite an important skill.  Certainly, there’s work to do from the faculty and instructor side: to make sure that our recitations are maximally useful; to make sure that our office hours are serving students in the best way possible; to encourage the students and try to remind them that they have some responsibility for their education, and that the best way is to come and show up and interact with the material. But we should also recognize our responsibility to the students to deliver them the best learning experience possible and to give them an educational system that challenges them but also is a quality product they want to come and take part in. Q: Why would you still encourage students to pursue studies in mathematics given the advances AI technologies have made? Do you still see the future of mathematics as exciting? A: Yes, for a multitude of reasons. The act of learning how to think is going to be more important than ever. This idea of being an expert, of knowing all these things, which are easily available and at your fingertips, is perhaps a little less important when you have a machine that has all these resources. I think something that may become even more important is the ability to think for yourself. Because with the existence of these machines, I think a natural fear is that that skill set is going to lessen in the general population as generations move on and on, and so I think that ability will be at a premium. I think training in mathematics and quantitative sciences more generally is quite important for that.  The second thing is community. I think learning, not by yourself, but with a group of peers, greatly improves the overall experience. It’s an integral part of the experience. I would say those two things are the reason why I think it’s still important to study math, to study quantitative sciences, and also why it’s still important to come and go to class.  The world is changing fairly rapidly. I think we as an institution have a responsibility to prepare students for that. We’re having lots of conversations about this right now because the ability to think, reason, and solve problems are core skills that our students, I think, will need now more than ever. I also think we need to make sure that we’re preparing our students for the world that they’re about to enter into. The exact way that we teach our students, or prepare our students for the world, absolutely cannot look like what it was 10 years ago. Because this world simply looks quite different.
1ac3744caa9c0983: When deploying deep learning models in high-stakes scenarios, researchers would like to understand how they work. Today, this requires unraveling an enormously complex network of internal processing nodes to understand what the model knows and how it will likely behave in practice. Jacob Andreas would rather have the models explain themselves.  The newly tenured associate professor develops techniques that enable artificial intelligence models to communicate accurately about what they learned from their training data, in language humans can understand. “Rather than needing to use all these external tools to try and understand what is going on under the hood, maybe we can train models to talk about themselves in a way that is accurate,” says Andreas, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). By studying how machines come to understand language, Andreas and his group work toward building intelligent systems that can learn about the world from human guidance and communicate effectively with human collaborators. They develop methods to make the training process more natural and efficient, so AI models learn in a way that is more like human learning. Ultimately, he and his group want to help people design more accurate and robust deep-learning models that are better suited for their intended application.  “We used to debug systems just by looking at their parameters and figuring out whether they make sense or not. Now, we need ‘mind-reading tools’ that can take this really complicated neural computation and translate it for us because it is just not in a language that we, as humans, know how to speak,” he says. A love of language Andreas’ fascination with language blossomed at a young age. As a child growing up in the San Francisco Bay Area, he was a voracious reader of any book he could get his hands on.  One such book, passed along to him by a family friend, contained a pivotal scene where the main character hacked into a computer system to save the day. That piqued his interest in computers. A few years later, his father brought home a simple BASIC Engine that Andreas could run on their home computer, and he started immersing himself in the world of computer programming. Andreas chose to major in computer science as an undergraduate at Columbia University but wasn’t sure if he wanted to pursue a career as a researcher, as a software engineer, or at a startup. His friends signed up for research projects in faculty labs, so Andreas figured he would try that, too. “I just blast emailed everyone in the computer science department who was working on anything vaguely AI-related, and the natural language processing faculty got back to me first. That is how I wound up in the field where I am now,” he says. Working in the lab of Michael Collins, the Vikram S. Pandit Professor of Computer Science at Columbia University, Andreas completed an undergraduate thesis project on machine translation. His project involved adapting existing statistical techniques for representing the meaning of language into more powerful AI systems that could translate passages of text. “I always felt like these deeper questions about how thought works or how to model the world were closer to the surface in language processing problems than in the other tasks that AI people were working on at the time,” he recalls. A seismic shift He wanted to keep exploring deep questions, so Andreas enrolled in graduate school at the University of California at Berkeley to pursue a career as an academic researcher.  Before starting his PhD studies, he spent a year earning a master’s degree at Cambridge University in England. In that historic environment, he was inspired to contemplate the nature of language learning as he worked on computational translation problems. Those studies fueled his research when he joined the lab of Berkeley professor of computer science Dan Klein.  Andreas began his studies at the time when neural networks were starting to take off. The field of natural language processing was making a seismic shift from statistical methods to this new world of deep learning.  Statistical methods utilize transparent, mathematical formulas to analyze text, while deep learning techniques use opaque algorithms to automatically learn complex meanings from massive amounts of text data. “It was fun to be there as we made this transition to the modern toolkit, and learning and inventing all of that stuff when it was still new,” Andreas says. He began collaborating with scientists in computer vision labs to tackle increasingly complex questions about language learning. Together, they designed AI systems that excelled at generating natural language by teaching those systems to “see” and understand the world around them.  “This was all super-exciting because there really hadn’t been a common set of tools for working with both language and vision data. Then, all of a sudden, neural networks gave us this common language,” he recalls. He completed a thesis project on the use of neural module networks, which are small fragments of neural networks that perform specific tasks, like localizing objects or logical reasoning, in a larger AI system. But it was the more speculative projects he tackled alongside his thesis, like interpretability and creating natural language descriptions of an AI model’s internal states, that would drive the focus of his group at MIT. Faculty focus After spending a year at the startup Semantic Machines (which spun out of his lab at Berkeley), Andreas joined the MIT faculty in 2019. “It felt like this was a fantastic opportunity to be in the homeland of AI research and collaborate with all these amazing, established people, but also do something new and figure out what the modern era in machine learning was going to look like,” he says. His group focuses on two main areas. First, they are studying the science of large language models to understand the algorithms these models deploy as they learn and process information.  The tools they develop help scientists and researchers better predict how a trained model will behave in the real world. For instance, one family of techniques they developed trains large language models to explain what is going on inside other neural networks using language a human could understand.  These techniques can assign a natural language description to every information-processing node in a massive neural network. For example, one such description might represent an individual node that identifies “patches of grass near animals” in input images.  “That work serves as a jumping off point for a bunch of higher-level questions we ask about how these models represent meaning,” he says. On the other side, his team designs new algorithms for training machine-learning models, and for predicting how specific datasets or examples will affect different aspects of model behavior.  “We don’t have a good scientific theory of what is going to happen when you train a model on a particular dataset. This is a big challenge for the field right now,” he says. A changing environment The speed of AI advancement presents one of the biggest challenges his lab faces. The field seems to completely change every three to five years, Andreas says, forcing him to stay nimble and ready to learn something new. That same dilemma carries over into the courses 6.461 and 6.861 (undergraduate and graduate Natural Language Processing), which Andreas co-teaches. He and his fellow instructors must redesign the course each year to keep up with the newest developments. It’s also challenging to teach the technical pieces of machine learning in an era where every assignment could be completed by a large language model rather than a human pupil. “I try to impress upon the students that having a really deep foundation in how all this technology works under the hood is the only way they are going to understand it, and will differentiate them in a world where everyone has access to a coding agent,” he says. With so much change, it is difficult to predict where the field is headed next, Andreas says. He foresees that his group’s work on interpretability will become even more important for making advanced systems like AI agents safe enough to deploy in high-stakes situations. This will be especially true as researchers design deep-learning models that can aid in scientific discovery. These models will be trained on troves of raw data from research labs that may not be well-understood by scientists yet.  “Figuring out how to enable these models to verbalize all of this hidden knowledge they have about things people have never written about explicitly will be a huge challenge and opportunity for people who work in machine learning,” he says. In addition to tackling challenges in the lab, Andreas enjoys pushing himself as a hiker and backpacker. He has loved spending time in the outdoors since his childhood in California and goes on at least one or two backpacking trips each summer. He and a colleague in the Department of Mathematics are working their way across all the 4,000-foot peaks in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, making slow but steady progress. And now that he has earned tenure, Andreas is looking forward to getting back into an old hobby — singing in a chamber choir. He’s always enjoyed music and became enamored with chapel choirs and bell ringing during his time at Cambridge University.
51629ce4bfc0b4a3: Belum pun genap sehari selepas artikel saya yang mempersoalkan kewibawaan Ismail Lasim dan 10 bekas ahli Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri (exco) yang cuba menyingkirkan Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan diterbitkan, muncul satu perkembangan mengejutkan.
Secara tiba-tiba, Setiausaha Agung Barisan Nasional (BN) Zambry Abd Kadir mengumumkan secara rasmi Ismail telah meletakkan jawatan.
Reaksi pertama saya adalah lega. Pada pandangan saya, keputusan Adun Juasseh itu untuk berundur membuka peluang kepada Negeri Sembilan memulakan lembaran baharu.

Apa yang berlaku sejak beberapa minggu lalu meninggalkan kesan mendalam terhadap landskap politik dan adat istiadat negeri itu. Cubaan mencabar kedudukan Yang Dipertuan Besar sudah melampaui batas yang sukar dimaafkan oleh ramai rakyat Malaysia, tanpa mengira fahaman politik.

Justeru, peletakan jawatan Ismail membuka ruang memulihkan hubungan antara kerajaan negeri dan institusi diraja, sekali gus membolehkan kedua-dua pihak bergerak ke hadapan dalam semangat perdamaian dan kestabilan.

Dalam hal ini, pengunduran Ismail boleh dianggap sebagai satu pengorbanan, walaupun beliau hanya memegang jawatan menteri besar untuk tempoh yang amat singkat. Jika keputusan itu dapat mengembalikan keyakinan rakyat dan memelihara keharmonian negeri, maka langkah tersebut wajar dihargai.
Namun, peletakan jawatan semata-mata belum memadai.

Ismail dan 10 bekas exco yang bersama-sama dengannya dalam kemelut ini juga perlu secara terbuka menjauhkan diri daripada mana-mana kelompok dalam institusi adat yang masih enggan mengakui kesalahan mereka.

Jika mereka terus berdiam diri, pelbagai persoalan akan terus timbul. Sekiranya benar-benar menyesal, mereka perlu menyatakannya dengan jelas dan tanpa berselindung. Rakyat Negeri Sembilan berhak mendapat jaminan bahawa tindakan luar biasa yang mencerminkan ketidaksetiaan dan kurangnya rasa hormat terhadap Yang Dipertuan Besar tidak akan berulang.
Walaupun perkembangan ini membawa kelegaan dan membuka peluang untuk memulakan lembaran baharu, masih terdapat beberapa persoalan yang belum terjawab.

Persoalan paling jelas ialah mengapa baru sekarang? Mengapa Ismail tidak mengumumkan sendiri peletakan jawatannya? Mengapa berita itu disampaikan oleh setiausaha agung BN, bukannya oleh beliau sendiri sebagai menteri besar?

Lebih penting, mengapa keputusan itu diumumkan sebelum Ismail menghadap Tuanku Muhriz, sedangkan beliau dilaporkan telah memohon perkenan untuk menghadap baginda selepas menyerahkan surat menarik balik usaha terdahulu untuk menyingkirkan pemerintah negeri itu?
Persoalan ini penting kerana masa sesuatu keputusan dibuat kadangkala dapat memberikan gambaran tentang sebab di sebalik tindakan tersebut.

Sekiranya Ismail terlebih dahulu menghadap Tuanku Muhriz dan permohonan maafnya tidak mendapat sambutan yang diharapkan, keputusan untuk meletakkan jawatan tentu lebih mudah difahami, malah mungkin dianggap sebagai langkah yang terhormat.

Dalam keadaan itu, seseorang menteri besar mungkin menyedari bahawa hubungan kepercayaan yang diperlukan untuk mentadbir negeri sudah terlalu terjejas dan sukar dipulihkan. Jika itulah urutan peristiwa yang berlaku, keputusan berundur mempunyai asas politik dan moral yang lebih jelas.
Namun, apa yang berlaku adalah sebaliknya. Pengumuman peletakan jawatan dibuat terlebih dahulu.

Urutan peristiwa yang luar biasa ini menimbulkan pelbagai persoalan. Adakah keputusan berundur benar-benar datang daripada Ismail sendiri? Atau adakah beliau menerima cadangan, galakan atau mungkin tekanan daripada pihak lain yang merasakan kemelut itu sudah sampai ke tahap memerlukan campur tangan segera?
Saya tidak mempunyai jawapan kepada persoalan itu. Namun, sukar untuk tidak tertanya-tanya tentang keadaan yang membawa kepada pengumuman berkenaan.

Dalam kemelut politik seperti yang kita saksikan, ada masanya persengketaan lama perlu diketepikan demi kepentingan bersama. Namun, perdamaian yang benar-benar bermakna memerlukan kejelasan, ketelusan dan kebertanggungjawaban.
Ia tidak boleh bergantung semata-mata pada kenyataan yang menunjukkan niat baik. Rakyat berhak mengetahui bagaimana konflik serius ini tercetus dan mengapa ia berakhir secara begitu mendadak.
Perkara ini lebih penting kerana keseluruhan kemelut itu tidak menggambarkan kepimpinan yang tenang dan matang dalam membuat keputusan.

Sekiranya permohonan maaf dibuat lebih awal, banyak ketidakpastian mungkin dapat dielakkan. Rakyat juga tidak perlu melalui ketegangan politik dan keadaan yang memalukan institusi negeri selama berminggu-minggu.

Sebaliknya, kemelut itu berlarutan sehingga menghampiri persidangan DUN, sekali gus menimbulkan tanggapan bahawa tindakan yang diambil lebih didorong oleh desakan politik yang semakin kuat, bukannya penyesalan yang ikhlas.
Dalam memegang jawatan awam, persepsi rakyat juga penting.

Seseorang pemimpin bukan hanya dinilai berdasarkan keputusan akhir yang dibuat, tetapi juga sejauh mana beliau cepat menyedari kesilapan dan mengambil langkah membetulkannya, walaupun terpaksa menanggung kerugian sendiri.
Sebaliknya, penyesalan yang hanya ditunjukkan selepas sekian lama boleh dilihat bukan sebagai tanda rendah diri, tetapi seolah-olah tindakan yang dibuat setelah mengambil kira kepentingan tertentu.
Namun, apa yang berlaku sudah pun berlaku. Keutamaan sekarang mestilah kebajikan Negeri Sembilan dan rakyatnya.

Persaingan antara kelompok politik, cita-cita peribadi dan pertelingkahan antara institusi tidak seharusnya mengatasi tanggungjawab lebih besar untuk mentadbir negeri dengan baik. Negeri Sembilan memerlukan kestabilan, pentadbiran yang cekap dan komitmen baharu untuk berkhidmat kepada rakyat.
Paling penting, negeri itu memerlukan hubungan yang sihat dan saling menghormati antara kerajaan negeri dengan institusi istana.

Walau apa pun pandangan politik seseorang, Yang Dipertuan Besar kekal sebagai lambang penting kesinambungan, kewibawaan dan kepimpinan berteraskan nilai moral dalam kerangka perlembagaan serta adat Negeri Sembilan yang tersendiri.
Saya berharap menteri besar baharu akan menjalankan tanggungjawabnya dengan pemahaman dan penghargaan yang lebih mendalam terhadap peranan tersebut.
Negeri Sembilan telah melalui satu episod yang tidak sepatutnya berlaku dan amat dikesali. Namun, setiap krisis juga membuka peluang untuk melakukan pembaharuan.

Kita tidak harus lupa kuasa politik hanya bersifat sementara, sedangkan kepercayaan rakyat dan keutuhan institusi jauh lebih penting serta berkekalan. Jika mereka yang diberi amanah memimpin dapat mengambil pengajaran daripada kemelut ini, mungkin masih ada hikmah yang boleh diperoleh daripada peristiwa tersebut.

Dengan harapan itu, saya berdoa agar kebijaksanaan mengatasi segala pertelingkahan, keyakinan rakyat dapat dipulihkan dan Negeri Sembilan terus melangkah ke hadapan sebagai sebuah negeri yang bersatu, stabil dan lebih kukuh daripada sebelumnya.
Semoga tuhan memberikan petunjuk kepada kita semua.
